Understanding Anemia
A Public Health Awareness Reference for Women and Adolescent Girls
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Anemia is a condition in which the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or enough haemoglobin, the substance in blood that carries oxygen to all parts of the body. When the body's tissues and organs do not get enough oxygen, a person can feel weak, tired, and less able to carry out daily activities. Anemia is one of the most common health problems in the world, and it affects women and girls far more than men.

Growing children, menstruating adolescent girls, and pregnant or breastfeeding women need more iron and nutrients than others, which makes them more likely to develop anemia if their diet or health does not meet these extra needs. Anemia is largely preventable and treatable. With a balanced diet, timely health check-ups, and awareness of warning signs, most cases can be prevented or corrected before they become serious. Common Symptoms
Anemia often develops slowly, so early signs may be mild and easy to overlook.

Common Symptoms
Anemia often develops slowly, so early signs may be mild and easy to overlook. Common symptoms include:
Constant tiredness or weakness, even after rest
Pale skin, lips, nails, or the inside of the eyelids
Shortness of breath, especially during physical activity
Dizziness or light-headedness
Fast or irregular heartbeat
Headaches
Difficulty concentrating or reduced alertness
Cold hands and feet
Brittle nails or hair thinning
Unusual cravings to eat non-food items such as mud, chalk, or ice (a sign sometimes seen in severe iron deficiency)
In adolescent girls and women, these symptoms are sometimes mistaken for normal tiredness. Because anemia is common and often overlooked, a simple blood test at a health centre is the best way to confirm it.

Causes
Anemia can develop for several reasons, and more than one cause is often present at the same time:
Not eating enough iron-rich foods, such as green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery, and non-vegetarian foods where consumed
Low intake of foods rich in folic acid and vitamin B12
Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding
Pregnancy and breastfeeding, which greatly increase the body's need for iron and nutrients
Frequent infections or intestinal worm infestations, which can cause blood loss or poor nutrient absorption
Poor absorption of iron due to certain digestive conditions
Chronic illnesses or long-term infections
Inherited blood disorders, in some cases
Repeated childbirth with little gap between pregnancies, without adequate nutritional recovery
Adolescent girls are especially at risk because their bodies are growing rapidly while also losing blood through monthly periods, which increases their need for iron at a time when dietary habits may not meet this demand.

When to See a Doctor
Any woman or girl with ongoing tiredness, paleness, or the other symptoms listed above should visit the nearest health centre for a simple blood test.

In addition, the following signs need urgent medical attention and should not be ignored:
Severe weakness or inability to carry out daily activities
Fainting or repeated dizziness
Chest pain, a racing heart, or severe breathlessness, even at rest
Very pale skin, lips, or nails that develop suddenly
Heavy vaginal bleeding, whether during periods or pregnancy
Bleeding that will not stop, or blood in stool or vomit
Anemia identified during pregnancy, especially in later months
Rapid breathing or swelling of the feet along with tiredness
Yellowing of the eyes or skin along with weakness
If any of these red-flag signs appear, the person should be taken to the nearest hospital or Primary Health Centre (PHC) as soon as possible.
Untreated severe anemia can affect the heart and, particularly in pregnancy, can be dangerous for both mother and baby.

Home Care and Prevention
Most cases of anemia, especially those caused by poor diet, can be prevented through everyday habits and awareness:
Iron-Rich and Balanced Diet
Eat more green leafy vegetables (such as spinach and drumstick leaves), pulses, beans, jaggery, and seasonal fruits
Include eggs, fish, or meat where dietary habits allow, as these are rich sources of iron
Eat foods rich in vitamin C, such as citrus fruits, guava, or tomatoes, alongside iron-rich meals, as this helps the body absorb iron better
Limit tea or coffee immediately before or after meals, as this can reduce iron absorption
Health and Hygiene Habits
Take part in government deworming programmes, as intestinal worms can worsen anemia
Maintain good hygiene and clean drinking water to reduce infections
Get adequate rest and avoid overexertion when feeling weak
Drink enough fluids through the day, particularly during pregnancy or breastfeeding
Awareness for Adolescent Girls and Women
Take part in school or community programmes that provide iron and folic acid supplements, where offered by health workers
Girls and women should get their haemoglobin checked periodically, especially during adolescence and pregnancy
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should attend all recommended antenatal and postnatal check-ups
Family members and communities should encourage girls to eat nutritious meals rather than eating last or eating less, a pattern that is still common in some households
This document does not cover medicines, supplements, or dosages.

Any decisions about iron or folic acid supplementation and treatment must be made only by a qualified doctor or health worker. Odisha-Specific Notes
Anemia among women and adolescent girls is a well-recognised public health priority in Odisha, particularly in the state's tribal and rural belts, where nutritional gaps and limited access to health services can add to the risk.

Free haemoglobin testing, iron and folic acid supplementation, and deworming services are available through government health centres, schools, and Anganwadi centres under national programmes such as Anemia Mukt Bharat
ASHA and Anganwadi workers in Odisha play an important role in identifying anemia early, distributing supplements, and guiding families to the nearest health facility
Locally available foods such as green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery, ragi (mandia), and seasonal fruits can support better iron intake and are encouraged as part of community nutrition efforts
Adolescent girls in schools and out-of-school settings are encouraged to take part in weekly iron and folic acid supplementation programmes run through health and education departments
Families in tribal and remote areas are encouraged to use local health camps, Health and Wellness Centres, and mobile health units for regular check-ups, especially during pregnancy
Community awareness, regular check-ups, and access to nutritious food remain key to reducing anemia among women and girls across the state.

Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY)
India's National Health Insurance Scheme, Explained Simply
A Public Awareness Reference Guide
1. Overview
Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) is a health insurance scheme run by the Government of India. Its purpose is to help poor and vulnerable families get hospital treatment without worrying about the cost. The scheme was launched in September 2018 and is managed by the National Health Authority (NHA), under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. PM-JAY gives eligible families cashless and paperless treatment at government and private hospitals that are registered, or "empanelled", under the scheme. This means a family does not need to pay money upfront or later claim reimbursement; the hospital is paid directly by the scheme.

PM-JAY is described as one of the largest government-funded health insurance schemes in the world, and it works alongside Health and Wellness Centres, which provide routine and preventive care closer to home. 2. Eligibility
PM-JAY does not require families to pay a premium. Eligibility is largely based on the Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC 2011) data, which identifies deprived rural and urban households. Broadly, a family may be eligible if it fits into certain deprivation categories, such as:
Rural households living in a kutcha (temporary or poorly built) house with only one room, or with no adult family member between 16 and 59 years of age. Households headed by a woman with no adult male member in the family, or families with a disabled member and no able-bodied adult.

Families that depend mainly on manual casual labour, or belong to specific marginalised or landless categories identified in the SECC data. In urban areas, eligibility is generally linked to specific occupational categories, such as street vendors, rag pickers, domestic workers, construction workers, and similar informal-sector occupations identified under the scheme. In a more recent expansion, all senior citizens aged 70 years and above have been made eligible for PM-JAY coverage, regardless of their family's income, under a separate Ayushman Vay Vandana Card. Senior citizens who already have coverage under schemes like CGHS or ECHS can choose to continue with their existing scheme or switch to PM-JAY, but cannot use both at the same time.

Because eligibility is based on official databases and criteria that can be updated, families should not assume they are covered or excluded without checking. The scheme has its own online tool to confirm this individually. 3. Benefits
PM-JAY offers a defined package of benefits designed to reduce the financial burden of hospital treatment:
Health cover of up to five lakh rupees per family, per year, for hospital treatment. This amount is meant to be used as needed and is not divided per person; the whole family can draw from the same cover. No restriction on family size, age, or gender; every member of an eligible family can be covered under one entitlement. Coverage for pre-existing illnesses from the very first day, unlike many private insurance policies that apply a waiting period.

Cashless treatment at empanelled hospitals anywhere in the country, not just in the beneficiary's home state, which is useful for migrant workers and families who travel. Coverage for a wide range of medical and surgical procedures, including common surgeries, cancer treatment, dialysis for kidney patients, newborn and child care, and many other secondary and tertiary care services. Related expenses such as consultation, diagnostic tests, and medicines are generally covered for a short period before hospitalisation and after discharge, in addition to the hospital stay itself.

The exact list of covered procedures, package rates, and any recent additions are decided and periodically updated by the National Health Authority, so it is best to confirm current details for a specific treatment directly with an empanelled hospital or the official portal. 4. How to Apply
Step 1: Check Eligibility
Eligibility can be checked online through the official PM-JAY beneficiary portal or the Ayushman App, using a registered mobile number. After verifying the number with an OTP, the applicant selects their state and district and searches using details such as Aadhaar number, ration card number, or household ID to see if the family appears in the beneficiary list.

Step 2: Complete e-KYC and Get the Ayushman Card
If the family is listed as eligible, the applicant can proceed to complete e-KYC (identity verification) using Aadhaar, through OTP or biometric verification. Once e-KYC is completed, the Ayushman card can be generated and downloaded online, or printed with help from a nearby Common Service Centre (CSC), empanelled hospital, or Ayushman Mitra. Families without internet access can visit their nearest Common Service Centre, empanelled government hospital, or local health facility for assistance with checking eligibility and completing the process.

Step 3: Use the Card for Treatment
When hospital treatment is needed, the beneficiary can visit any empanelled hospital, show the Ayushman card along with identity proof, and receive treatment on a cashless basis for covered procedures. Hospital staff or an Ayushman Mitra posted at the hospital usually assist with verification and paperwork at this stage. Because processes and portals are updated from time to time, it is advisable to keep Aadhaar, ration card, and other identity documents ready, and to confirm the latest application steps on the official website before applying. 5. Biju Swasthya Kalyan Yojana (BSKY)
Odisha's State Health Assurance Scheme, Explained Simply
A Public Awareness Reference Guide
Important update: Since early 2025, BSKY has been rebranded by the Government of Odisha as the Gopabandhu Jan Arogya Yojana (GJAY), which is now integrated with the central Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY scheme. Readers should confirm on the official Odisha Health and Family Welfare portal whether their card or benefits are currently referred to as BSKY or GJAY, as names and processes may have changed since this document was written. 1. Overview
Biju Swasthya Kalyan Yojana (BSKY) is a state health assurance scheme launched by the Government of Odisha, named after the state's former Chief Minister, Biju Patnaik.

It was introduced to reduce the financial burden of hospital treatment on the people of Odisha, especially those from economically weaker sections. BSKY works in two parts. The first part provides completely free treatment to every resident of Odisha, regardless of income, at all state government health facilities, from the sub-centre level up to district headquarters hospitals and government medical colleges. The second part provides cashless health insurance-style coverage for treatment at empanelled private hospitals, mainly for families holding a ration card under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) or the State Food Security Scheme (SFSS). 2.

2. Eligibility
Every resident of Odisha, regardless of income or social category, is eligible for free treatment at state government hospitals and health centres under the first part of BSKY. For cashless treatment at empanelled private hospitals under the second part, eligibility is generally linked to holding a valid NFSA or SFSS ration card, which serves as the basis for BSKY coverage rather than a separate BSKY database. There is no specific age limit for availing BSKY benefits, and coverage applies to the whole family listed on the ration card. Because BSKY does not require a separate income or category-based application for most families, many households are automatically considered eligible once their ration card details are verified. 3.

3. Benefits
Health coverage of up to five lakh rupees per family per year, with an enhanced limit of up to ten lakh rupees for women beneficiaries, for treatment costs within Odisha. Cashless treatment at a network of empanelled government and private hospitals, so families do not need to pay upfront and later claim reimbursement. Coverage for a large number of surgical procedures and medical treatments, including major illnesses, without requiring a specific waiting period, and generally without a cap on room rent. Coverage for pre-existing health conditions from the time the card becomes active, similar in spirit to central schemes. Support is available through Swasthya Mitras or similar help-desk staff posted at hospitals to assist beneficiaries with the process.

The exact list of covered procedures, hospital network, and financial limits may be revised periodically by the state government, so beneficiaries should confirm current details for their specific treatment need directly with an empanelled hospital or the official portal. 4. How to Apply
In most cases, there is no separate enrolment process for BSKY. Families already covered under NFSA or SFSS ration cards are automatically considered eligible and are expected to receive a BSKY smart health card. Check whether your family already has a BSKY smart health card at home; this is usually distributed by the state government along with information campaigns.

If the card has not been received, visit the nearest Mo Seva Kendra (a citizen service centre) with your NFSA or SFSS ration card to request the BSKY card. For treatment, visit any empanelled government or private hospital, show your BSKY card (or the ration card, where accepted) along with identity proof, and hospital staff or a Swasthya Mitra will assist with verification. For queries or to check claim status, beneficiaries can contact the official helpline numbers or use the state's official health portal or app. 5.

5. How BSKY Compares with Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY)
For several years after the central Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY scheme was launched in 2018, the Odisha government chose to run BSKY as its own separate state scheme rather than adopting PM-JAY, citing BSKY's coverage for all residents at government facilities and its higher coverage limit for women as reasons for the state's approach. From 2025 onwards, Odisha has joined Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY and integrated it with its own state scheme, now referred to as the Gopabandhu Jan Arogya Yojana (GJAY).

Under this integrated arrangement, families in Odisha are intended to benefit from both the central government's funding and hospital network under PM-JAY, as well as the state-specific features that BSKY previously offered, such as free care at all government facilities and enhanced coverage for women. Because this transition is relatively recent, some processes, card names, and hospital networks may still be settling into place, so beneficiaries should verify their current entitlement and the correct scheme name with local health authorities. 6.

6. Source Basis

Chickenpox: A Public Health Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base
Overview
Chickenpox is a common illness caused by a virus called the varicella-zoster virus. It spreads very easily from one person to another and is most often seen in children, though adults who have never had it before can also get infected. The illness is known for an itchy rash that turns into small fluid-filled blisters, along with mild fever and tiredness. Most healthy children recover fully within one to two weeks with simple home care. However, chickenpox can be more serious in babies, adults, pregnant women, and people with weak immunity.

In India, including Odisha, chickenpox outbreaks are commonly seen in schools, hostels, anganwadi centres, and crowded households, especially where many children are in close contact with one another. Common Symptoms
Symptoms usually begin about two weeks after a person is exposed to someone with chickenpox, though this can range from ten days to three weeks.

Common symptoms include:
Mild fever, tiredness, and body ache before the rash appears
Loss of appetite and headache
An itchy rash that starts as small red spots, usually first on the chest, back, or face
The red spots turning into small blisters filled with clear fluid within a day or so
Blisters spreading to other parts of the body, including the scalp, mouth, and eyelids
Blisters gradually drying up and forming crusts or scabs over several days
New batches of spots may keep appearing for a few days, so a person may have spots, blisters, and scabs all at once
The illness usually lasts about a week to ten days from the time the rash first appears.

Once someone has had chickenpox, they usually do not get it again, though the virus stays quietly in the body and can cause a different illness called shingles later in life. Causes
Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus and spreads very easily between people, especially in schools, hostels, anganwadis, and crowded homes.

It spreads mainly through:
Coughing or sneezing, which releases tiny virus droplets into the air that others can breathe in
Direct contact with the fluid inside the blisters of an infected person
Touching objects, clothes, or bedding that have fresh fluid from the blisters on them, though this is less common than air and direct contact
Close contact with someone who has shingles, since the same virus can cause chickenpox in a person who has never had it before
A person with chickenpox can spread the infection to others from about one to two days before the rash appears until all the blisters have dried up and crusted over. This is why isolation during the infectious period is so important in controlling its spread.

When to See a Doctor (Red Flags)
Most cases of chickenpox are mild and can be managed at home. However, a doctor or the nearest health centre should be consulted promptly if any of the following are seen:
High fever that does not come down or lasts more than four days
Blisters that become red, swollen, warm, or filled with pus, which may mean a skin infection has developed
Severe headache, stiff neck, or unusual drowsiness
Difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or persistent cough
Repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down
Confusion, difficulty walking, or seizures
Bleeding into the blisters or unusual bruising on the skin
Chickenpox occurring in a newborn baby, a pregnant woman, an adult, or anyone with an existing illness or weak immunity
Signs of dehydration, such as very little urine, dry mouth, or sunken eyes
Newborns, pregnant women, adults who have never had chickenpox before, and people with conditions that weaken the immune system are at higher risk of complications and should seek medical advice as soon as symptoms appear, rather than waiting.

Home Care and Prevention
Caring for someone with chickenpox at home
Ensure plenty of rest until fever and tiredness settle down
Give enough fluids to drink to prevent dehydration
Offer light, simple meals if appetite is low
Keep fingernails short and clean to reduce skin damage and infection from scratching
Keep the skin clean; a lukewarm bath may help ease itching
Dress in loose, soft, breathable clothing
Do not give any medicine without a doctor's advice, and avoid unproven home remedies applied directly to the blisters
Watch for red-flag signs described above and seek medical care if they appear
Isolation and school exclusion during the infectious period
Because chickenpox spreads so easily, keeping an infected person away from others is one of the most effective ways to stop it from spreading further.

A person with chickenpox should stay at home and avoid close contact with others from the time symptoms start
Children should be kept away from school, anganwadi, or playgroups until every blister has fully dried and formed a scab, with no new blisters appearing
Adults with chickenpox should avoid the workplace and public gatherings during the same infectious period
Pregnant women, newborns, and people with weak immunity in the household should avoid contact with the infected person as much as possible
Inform the school, anganwadi, or workplace so that other contacts can be watched for early symptoms
Preventing chickenpox
Ask a doctor or health worker about the chickenpox vaccine, which can prevent infection or make the illness much milder
Avoid close contact with anyone currently showing chickenpox or shingles symptoms
Practice regular handwashing with soap and water
Avoid sharing towels, clothes, or bedding with an infected person
Odisha-Specific Notes
Chickenpox outbreaks are reported regularly across Odisha, and health surveillance data collected over the years shows that outbreaks have occurred in all districts of the state, with schools and anganwadi settings being frequent starting points because children are in close daily contact.

An outbreak investigated in the tribal district of Rayagada found that infection began in a residential school and then spread into the surrounding community, and it noted that local beliefs and traditional home remedies sometimes delayed proper isolation and care, allowing the illness to spread further. Case patterns across Odisha show that children between about six and twelve years of age are most commonly affected, though outbreaks involving adults, including in college hostels, have also been recorded.

For families and schools in Odisha, the following points are especially useful:
Because outbreaks often start in schools, anganwadis, and hostels, staff should watch for early signs like fever and rash and separate affected children promptly
In rural and tribal areas, traditional home remedies should not replace proper isolation, rest, fluids, and medical advice when red-flag symptoms appear
Any cluster of chickenpox-like illness in a school, hostel, or village should be reported early to the nearest health sub-centre, Anganwadi worker, or ASHA worker so the local health system can respond quickly
Discussing chickenpox vaccination with a doctor or at a local health facility can help reduce the size and severity of future outbreaks in schools and communities

Child Health Basics (0-5 Years)
A Public Health Awareness Reference on Growth Monitoring, Common Illnesses, and Immunization
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
The first five years of a child's life are the most important period for physical growth and brain development. Good nutrition, regular health check-ups, timely immunization, and prompt care during illness all help a child grow up healthy and strong. Young children are more vulnerable to infections and malnutrition because their immune systems and bodies are still developing.

Simple, regular practices at home, along with support from local health workers and Anganwadi centres, can help parents track their child's growth, recognise illness early, and protect against many serious diseases through vaccination. This document offers general awareness on growth monitoring, common childhood illnesses, and the importance of completing the full immunization schedule for children aged 0 to 5 years.

Key Practices
Growth Monitoring
Take the child for regular weight and height check-ups at the Anganwadi centre or health facility, as recommended by health workers
Keep the child's growth card or health record safely, and ensure it is updated at every visit
Watch for steady weight gain and growth over time; a flat or falling growth line can be an early sign of a health or nutrition problem
Discuss any concerns about the child's growth, appetite, or development with the Anganwadi worker, ASHA, or doctor
Ensure the child receives age-appropriate feeding: exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, followed by timely introduction of a variety of nutritious foods alongside continued breastfeeding
Recognising Common Childhood Illnesses
Diarrhoea: watch for frequent loose stools, and give oral rehydration solution (ORS) and continued fluids to prevent dehydration
Acute respiratory infections (cough, cold, pneumonia): watch for fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing, or persistent cough
Fever: monitor temperature, keep the child comfortable and hydrated, and seek care if fever is high, prolonged, or accompanied by other symptoms
Malnutrition: watch for low weight, visible thinness, or swelling of the feet, and seek help from the Anganwadi centre or health facility
Skin and eye infections: keep the child clean, wash hands and face regularly, and seek care if infection does not improve
Immunization
Ensure the child receives all vaccines under the government's routine immunization schedule, on time and in the correct sequence
Keep the child's vaccination card safely and bring it to every immunization session
Vaccines are provided free of cost at government health facilities, Anganwadi centres, and through outreach immunization sessions in villages
If a vaccine dose is missed, contact the local ASHA worker or health centre to catch up rather than skipping it altogether
Mild fever or soreness after vaccination is common and usually resolves on its own; consult a health worker if there are unusual or severe reactions
General Care at Home
Maintain good hygiene, including regular handwashing for the child and caregivers
Provide a balanced diet appropriate for the child's age, along with plenty of clean drinking water
Ensure adequate rest and a safe, clean environment for play and sleep
Seek prompt medical care for danger signs such as difficulty breathing, repeated vomiting, high fever, unusual drowsiness, or refusal to feed
Why It Matters
Regular growth monitoring helps identify malnutrition or health problems early, when they are easier to correct.

Children who are undernourished in early childhood are more likely to face long-term effects on their physical growth, learning ability, and overall health. Common childhood illnesses such as diarrhoea and respiratory infections remain leading causes of sickness and, if untreated, can become serious in young children. Recognising early warning signs and seeking timely care can prevent complications and save lives. Immunization protects children from serious, sometimes life-threatening diseases such as measles, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, and polio. When a child completes the full vaccination schedule, they are protected as an individual, and high immunization coverage in a community also helps protect other children, including those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons.

Together, growth monitoring, illness awareness, and immunization form the foundation of a healthy start in life, supporting a child's survival, growth, and development. Odisha-Specific Context
Odisha has an extensive network of Anganwadi centres under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, which plays a central role in supporting child health and nutrition across the state, including in rural and tribal areas.

Anganwadi workers in Odisha regularly monitor the growth of children under their care, weighing and measuring them and recording progress on growth charts to identify malnutrition early
Supplementary nutrition, health check-ups, and referral to Primary Health Centres are provided through Anganwadi centres for children found to be underweight or unwell
Routine immunization sessions are conducted at Anganwadi centres, Sub-Centres, and health facilities across Odisha as part of the national Universal Immunization Programme, with periodic special drives such as Mission Indradhanush reaching children who have missed scheduled vaccines
ASHA workers and Anganwadi workers together help families in remote and tribal areas access growth monitoring, immunization, and treatment for common childhood illnesses
Families in Odisha are encouraged to regularly visit their local Anganwadi centre for growth check-ups and to keep up to date with their child's immunization schedule
Making full use of local Anganwadi and health centre services gives children across Odisha the best chance at a healthy start in life.

Symptom Guide: Cold
A plain-language reference for community health awareness use
Symptom Overview
A 'cold' usually means a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, mild sore throat, and sometimes a mild cough or slight body ache. It is one of the most common health complaints and affects people of all ages, often more than once a year. Most colds are mild and go away on their own within about seven to ten days with rest and simple home care. This guide explains cold symptoms in general terms only. It does not identify a specific disease. It describes common reasons a cold may happen, simple things you can do at home, and signs that mean you should visit a health worker or doctor.

Possible Common Causes
A cold-like feeling can happen for several reasons, including:
Common viral infections of the nose and throat (the 'common cold'), which spread easily from person to person
Seasonal influenza (flu), which can feel similar to a cold but is often more severe
Sudden change in weather or temperature, especially during monsoon or winter months
Exposure to dust, smoke, or indoor cooking fumes
Seasonal allergies, such as reactions to pollen or dust
General tiredness or a weakened immune system due to poor sleep, stress, or inadequate nutrition
Close contact with someone who already has a cold or respiratory infection
This list only shows that many everyday factors can cause cold-like symptoms. It is not a way to diagnose yourself or another person.
It is not a way to diagnose yourself or another person. A trained health worker can assess the actual cause if the symptoms are severe or unusual.

A trained health worker can assess the actual cause if the symptoms are severe or unusual. Self-Care Advice
For a mild, ordinary cold without warning signs, the following steps can help you feel better while your body recovers:
Rest as much as possible and avoid heavy physical work until you feel better
Drink plenty of clean, safe (boiled or filtered) water and warm fluids such as soup or herbal tea
Gargle with warm salt water to ease a sore throat
Use steam inhalation (carefully, to avoid burns) to help relieve a blocked nose
Eat light, nutritious food, including fruits, to support recovery
Keep warm, especially during cold weather or after getting wet in the rain
Cover your nose and mouth when sneezing or coughing, and wash hands often to avoid spreading it to others
Avoid smoke, dust, and crowded closed spaces while unwell
A simple home remedy such as warm water with honey and ginger (avoid honey for infants under one year) may bring comfort if it is safe and familiar to the person
Most colds improve within a week to ten days without any special medicine.
If symptoms are getting worse instead of better after this time, it is best to get checked at a health facility.

When to Seek Medical Attention
Please visit the nearest health sub-centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital promptly if you or a family member notices any of the following:
High fever that does not come down, or fever lasting more than two to three days
Difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or shortness of breath
Chest pain or tightness
Symptoms that are not improving, or are getting worse, after seven to ten days
Severe sore throat, ear pain, or swelling in the neck
Persistent cough, especially if it lasts two weeks or more
Repeated vomiting, refusal to drink fluids, or signs of dehydration
Cold symptoms in a very young infant, elderly person, pregnant woman, or someone with an existing illness (such as diabetes, heart disease, or asthma)
Bluish lips or face, severe weakness, or confusion (seek emergency care immediately)
These signs may point to a more serious infection, such as influenza or a chest infection, which needs proper medical evaluation rather than home care alone.

Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, cold-like symptoms and seasonal respiratory illnesses tend to rise during the monsoon and winter months, when sudden weather changes, dampness, and indoor smoke exposure are more common in many households.

Free consultation and basic treatment for cold and fever symptoms are available at Health & Wellness Centres, PHCs, CHCs, and district hospitals across Odisha
ASHA and ANM workers in villages can guide families on home care and refer cases that need further medical attention
During winter, the Odisha Health Department advises keeping children, elderly people, and those with chronic illnesses (such as asthma or heart conditions) extra warm and away from cold winds, especially early morning and late evening
Good ventilation at home and reducing exposure to smoke from cooking fires can help lower the frequency of cold and respiratory symptoms
If cold symptoms are severe, prolonged, or affect a vulnerable family member, contact your nearest ASHA worker or health facility rather than waiting it out at home

content:
Common Cold and Influenza (Flu): A Public Health Awareness Guide
Simple information for families and communities
Overview
The common cold and influenza (flu) are both infections of the nose, throat, and airways caused by viruses. They spread very easily from person to person, especially in crowded places, schools, and homes. Although cold and flu can feel similar, flu is usually more severe and can, in some people, lead to serious complications. Both illnesses are very common and most people recover within one to two weeks with rest and simple home care. Because symptoms can sometimes overlap with other infections, it helps to know the warning signs that mean a person needs medical attention.

document_title: Common Cold and Flu Awareness Guide
content:
Common Symptoms
Cold and flu can cause similar symptoms, though flu tends to come on quickly and feel more severe. Common symptoms include:
Runny or blocked nose, and sneezing
Sore throat and cough
Mild to high fever
Headache
Body ache and tiredness
Chills or shivering
Loss of appetite
In some cases, mild breathlessness or chest discomfort
How to Tell the Difference: Cold vs Flu
Both illnesses affect the same parts of the body, but they usually differ in how they begin and how severe they feel. This simple comparison can help:
This is only a general guide, not a way to self-diagnose. If symptoms are severe, worsening, or unusual, a doctor should be consulted rather than guessing which illness it is.

document_title: Common Cold and Flu Awareness Guide
content:
Causes
Both cold and flu are caused by viruses, though different viruses are responsible for each. The common cold is usually caused by rhinoviruses, while flu is caused by influenza viruses. These viruses spread mainly through:
Droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes
Close contact with an infected person, such as shaking hands
Touching contaminated surfaces (doorknobs, utensils, mobile phones) and then touching the eyes, nose, or mouth
Crowded or poorly ventilated spaces, which allow viruses to spread quickly between people
In India, influenza tends to circulate more during two periods in the year — the monsoon months and the winter months — when crowding indoors and humidity or cold weather favour the spread of the virus.

document_title: Common Cold and Flu Awareness Guide
content:
When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs)
Most colds and many flu cases can be managed at home.

document_title: Common Cold and Flu Awareness Guide
content:
When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs)
Most colds and many flu cases can be managed at home. However, the following signs mean medical care should be sought promptly:
High fever that does not improve after 3 days, or fever that keeps returning
Difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or chest pain/tightness
Bluish colour of lips or face
Severe weakness, dizziness, or confusion
Symptoms that improve and then suddenly become worse again
Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down
Signs of dehydration (very little urine, dry mouth, extreme thirst)
Cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks or cough with blood
Fever or flu symptoms in a small infant, pregnant woman, elderly person, or someone with a chronic illness (such as heart, lung, or kidney disease, or diabetes)
Any symptom that feels unusually severe or is rapidly worsening
If any of these warning signs appear, visit the nearest doctor, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital without delay.

document_title: Common Cold and Flu Awareness Guide
content:
Home Care and Prevention
For mild cold or flu, the following home care measures can help recovery:
Take adequate rest and avoid strenuous work until fully recovered
Drink plenty of fluids — clean water, warm soups, and herbal drinks such as tulsi or ginger tea — to stay hydrated
Gargle with warm salt water to ease a sore throat
Eat light, nutritious food even if appetite is reduced
Keep the room warm, well ventilated, and free from smoke or dust
Cover the nose and mouth with a cloth or mask when coughing or sneezing
Avoid self-medicating with medicines bought without medical advice — consult a doctor or health worker for appropriate treatment
To help prevent cold and flu from spreading:
Wash hands frequently with soap and water, especially after coughing, sneezing, or touching shared surfaces
Avoid close contact with people who are sick, where possible
Cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing, using a tissue or the inner elbow
Avoid touching the eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
Keep living spaces clean and well ventilated
Eat a balanced diet, stay physically active, and get enough sleep to keep the immune system strong
Those who are sick should, where possible, stay home and avoid crowded places to prevent spreading the infection to others
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, cold and flu cases tend to follow the state's seasonal weather patterns:
Monsoon months (June to September): Frequent rain, humidity, and crowding indoors during heavy showers create favourable conditions for cold and flu viruses to spread, alongside other seasonal illnesses.

document_title: Common Cold and Flu Awareness Guide
content: Winter months (December to February): Cooler, drier weather in many parts of Odisha is commonly associated with a rise in respiratory infections, including cold and flu, particularly among children and elderly people. During both these seasons, crowded community settings such as markets, schools, and public transport can see faster spread of respiratory viruses, so simple hygiene practices become especially important. Residents are encouraged to seek care early at the nearest Anganwadi centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or government hospital if symptoms are severe or if a vulnerable family member (small child, elderly person, or pregnant woman) develops fever or breathing difficulty.

document_title: Conjunctivitis Eye Flu Public Health Reference
content:
Conjunctivitis ("Eye Flu")
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Overview
Conjunctivitis, commonly called "eye flu" or "pink eye," is a very common and highly contagious eye condition. It happens when the thin, clear layer covering the white part of the eye and the inside of the eyelids becomes red and swollen. Eye flu spreads quickly in families, schools, and crowded places, especially during certain times of the year. While it usually looks alarming because the eyes turn red and watery, most cases are mild and clear up on their own within a week or two with simple care. Because it spreads so easily, quick action and good hygiene are the best ways to protect yourself and others.

document_title: Conjunctivitis Eye Flu Public Health Reference
content:
Common Symptoms
Redness or pinkness in one or both eyes
Watering or excessive tearing
Itching, burning, or a gritty, uncomfortable feeling in the eye
Swelling of the eyelids
Discharge from the eye that may be clear, white, or yellowish, and can cause the eyelids to stick together, especially after sleep
Increased sensitivity to light in some cases
Mild general symptoms in some people, such as a sore throat, cold-like symptoms, or slight fever
Symptoms often begin in one eye and spread to the other within a day or two.

document_title: Conjunctivitis Eye Flu Public Health Reference
content:
Causes
Eye flu is usually caused by viruses, and less commonly by bacteria or allergies:
Viral conjunctivitis: the most common form, caused by common viruses; it is highly contagious and spreads through close contact, coughing, sneezing, or touching contaminated surfaces
Bacterial conjunctivitis: caused by bacteria, often with thicker yellow-green discharge and crusting; also contagious
Allergic conjunctivitis: caused by dust, pollen, smoke, or other irritants; it is not contagious and usually affects both eyes with itching
The infectious forms spread easily through direct contact with an infected person, by touching the eyes with unwashed hands, or by sharing items such as towels, handkerchiefs, pillows, or spectacles that have come into contact with infected discharge.

document_title: Conjunctivitis Eye Flu Public Health Reference
content:
When to See a Doctor (Red Flags)
Most cases of eye flu are mild, but a person should see a doctor or visit the nearest health centre promptly if any of the following occur:
Severe pain in the eye, not just mild discomfort or itching
Noticeable change or blurring in vision
Strong sensitivity to light that makes it hard to keep the eyes open
Thick, heavy discharge that keeps building up, or the eye appears to have a white spot or ulcer
Symptoms in a newborn baby or very young child
No improvement after 5–7 days, or symptoms getting worse instead of better
High fever along with the eye symptoms
History of recent eye injury or eye surgery
Home Care and Prevention
Wash hands frequently with soap and water, especially before and after touching the eyes or face
Avoid touching or rubbing the infected eye(s)
Gently clean discharge from the eyes using a clean, soft cloth or cotton, using a fresh one for each eye
Use a clean, cool or lukewarm damp cloth over closed eyes for comfort
Do not share towels, handkerchiefs, pillows, spectacles, or eye makeup with others
Wash bedsheets, pillow covers, and towels regularly in hot water and dry them in sunlight where possible
Avoid going to school, work, or crowded public places while symptoms and discharge are present, to prevent spreading infection to others
Do not use contact lenses until the eyes have fully recovered
Get adequate rest and drink enough fluids to support recovery, especially if there is fever or general body ache
Do not use any eye drops, ointment, or home remedy without guidance from a qualified health worker or doctor, as the wrong treatment can worsen certain types of eye infection
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, conjunctivitis cases typically rise sharply during the monsoon season, when high humidity, waterlogging, and crowded indoor gatherings create ideal conditions for the infection to spread.

document_title: Conjunctivitis Eye Flu Public Health Reference
content: Odisha's Health and Family Welfare Department has, in past monsoon seasons, issued public advisories after noting a significant increase in conjunctivitis cases across several districts, and has urged people to maintain hand and eye hygiene and to avoid close contact with infected persons. Schools are a common site of rapid spread among children, so health authorities have advised that children showing symptoms of eye flu stay home and avoid school until they recover, to protect classmates. Shared use of handkerchiefs, towels, and water sources in crowded households and community settings can also speed up transmission during this period.

document_title: Conjunctivitis Eye Flu Public Health Reference
content:
During the monsoon months, extra attention to hand-washing, avoiding face-touching, and seeking care early at the nearest sub-centre, primary health centre, or community health worker can help limit the spread of eye flu within families and communities in the state. Source Basis

Symptom Guide: Cough
A plain-language reference for community health awareness use
Symptom Overview
Cough is one of the most common symptoms that brings people to a health worker or clinic. It is the body's natural way of clearing the throat and airways of dust, mucus, smoke, or germs. Most coughs are mild and go away on their own within one to two weeks. However, a cough can sometimes be a sign of an infection or other health problem that needs attention, especially if it lasts a long time or comes with other symptoms. This guide describes cough in general terms. It does not tell you what disease you have. It only explains common reasons a cough may happen, simple steps you can take at home, and signs that mean you should see a health worker or doctor without delay.

Possible Common Causes
A cough can happen for many reasons. Some common ones include:
Common cold or seasonal flu (viral infection of the nose and throat)
Dust, smoke, indoor cooking fumes, or other irritants in the air
Seasonal allergies (reaction to pollen, dust mites, or similar triggers)
Throat irritation from dry air or talking/shouting for long periods
Chest infections such as bronchitis or pneumonia
Ongoing lung conditions such as asthma or chronic bronchitis
Acid reflux (stomach acid rising into the throat)
A cough that lasts two weeks or longer can, in some cases, be linked to tuberculosis (TB), which is an important public health concern in India
This list is only meant to show that many different things can cause a cough. It is not a way to diagnose yourself or anyone else.
It is not a way to diagnose yourself or anyone else. Only a qualified health worker can determine the actual cause after examination and, if needed, tests.

Self-Care Advice
For a mild, recent cough without warning signs, the following steps may bring comfort while your body recovers:
Drink plenty of clean, safe (boiled or filtered) water and warm fluids
Rest well and avoid overexertion
Gargle with warm salt water to soothe throat irritation
Avoid smoke, dust, and strong fumes; keep the living area well-ventilated
Cover your mouth and nose with a cloth, tissue, or your elbow when coughing, and wash hands often
Avoid smoking and, where possible, second-hand smoke
Use a simple home remedy such as warm water with honey (avoid honey for infants under one year of age) if culturally practised and safe for the person
Wear a mask around others if you have an ongoing cough, to protect family members while the cause is being checked
If the cough does not improve within one to two weeks despite rest and home care, it is time to have it checked at a health facility.

When to Seek Medical Attention
Please visit the nearest health sub-centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital promptly if you notice any of the following:
Cough lasting two weeks or more
Blood in the cough or sputum
Difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or shortness of breath
Chest pain or tightness
High or persistent fever, especially with night sweats
Unexplained weight loss or ongoing loss of appetite
Cough in an infant, young child, elderly person, pregnant woman, or someone with an existing illness (such as diabetes, HIV, or malnutrition)
Bluish lips or face, or severe weakness/confusion (seek emergency care immediately)
A cough lasting two weeks or longer is a key warning sign for tuberculosis (TB) in India.

TB testing and treatment are provided free of cost at government health facilities under the national TB elimination programme. Getting checked early protects both your health and the health of your family. Odisha-Specific Notes
The Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare, through the State TB Cell and the National Health Mission, conducts regular community TB screening camps (Shivirs) across all districts, including rural and hard-to-reach areas, to find and treat people with prolonged cough early.

Free cough and TB screening is available at Health & Wellness Centres, PHCs, CHCs, and district hospitals across Odisha
Ni-kshay Mitras (community volunteers) and ASHA/ANM workers can help connect people with a persistent cough to the nearest testing centre
During monsoon and winter months, indoor smoke from cooking fires and damp housing conditions common in parts of rural Odisha can worsen coughs; improving ventilation at home can help
If you or a family member has had a cough for two weeks or more, ask your local ASHA worker or nearest health facility about free TB testing

Public Healthcare Facilities in Cuttack District, Odisha
A Structured Reference Guide to District, Community, and Primary Health Facilities
Overview
Cuttack district is one of Odisha's most populous and historically significant districts, and its headquarters town, Cuttack city, has long served as a major medical hub for the wider region — it hosts the SCB Medical College and Hospital, one of the oldest and largest tertiary-care government teaching hospitals in eastern India.

Below this tertiary tier, the district's public healthcare network follows the same tiered structure used across India: village-level Sub-Centres feed into Primary Health Centres (PHCs), which refer upward to Community Health Centres (CHCs), which in turn refer to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHH) as the district's secondary-level referral point. This structure is coordinated locally by the Chief District Medical Officer (CDMO), Cuttack, under the Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare, and follows standards set nationally through the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) via the National Health Mission (NHM), most recently revised in 2022.

Facility Types
District Headquarters Hospital (DHH), Cuttack
The DHH functions as the district's main secondary-level referral hospital, distinct from the tertiary-care SCB Medical College and Hospital located in the same city. It is intended to receive cases referred from CHCs, PHCs, and Sub-Centres across Cuttack district's blocks, and to provide a broader range of inpatient, diagnostic, and specialist services than block-level facilities. The exact current designation, address, and administrative details of the DHH should be confirmed with the CDMO Cuttack office, as this document does not independently verify facility-specific particulars.

Community Health Centres (CHCs)
CHCs are block-level referral units, generally built to serve a population of roughly 80,000 to 120,000 people, with lower population norms in hilly or tribal areas. Cuttack district's blocks (such as Athagarh, Banki, Salepur, Niali, Tangi-Choudwar, and others) are each expected to have a CHC serving as the referral point for PHCs within that block. A CHC is designed to have around 30 inpatient beds, an operation theatre, basic diagnostic and blood storage facilities, and specialist coverage in areas such as medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynaecology, and paediatrics, though actual staffing and equipment levels vary by centre. Centres equipped for round-the-clock emergency obstetric and newborn care may additionally be designated First Referral Units (FRUs).

Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
PHCs are typically the first point of contact with a qualified doctor for rural and semi-urban residents, each covering a population of around 20,000 to 30,000. A PHC supervises a cluster of Sub-Centres in its area and is expected to provide outpatient consultation, a small number of inpatient beds (around four to six), basic laboratory testing, and normal delivery services at PHCs designated for 24x7 care. PHCs also oversee ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) and ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwife) workers operating at the village level. Sub-Centres and Health & Wellness Centres
The most peripheral public health facilities are Health Sub-Centres, increasingly being upgraded as Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs).

These are generally staffed by an ANM and a Community Health Officer and focus on preventive and promotive care — immunization, antenatal check-ups, and basic screening — referring more complex cases upward to the PHC.

What Each Facility Handles
District Headquarters Hospital
Complex and emergency cases referred from CHCs and PHCs across the district
Broader specialist consultation and surgical services than block-level facilities
Diagnostics, blood storage/blood bank services, and larger inpatient bed capacity
Possible empanelment under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat–PM-JAY for cashless treatment (current empanelment status should be verified locally)
Acts as the secondary-level referral hospital for the district, with onward referral to SCB Medical College and Hospital or another tertiary centre for cases needing higher-level specialty or super-specialty care
Community Health Centres
Referral care for PHCs within the block, plus specialist consultation for patients approaching directly
Inpatient care (around 30 beds), minor and some major surgical procedures, and operation theatre services
Emergency obstetric care and institutional deliveries, particularly at centres designated as First Referral Units
Basic diagnostics including laboratory services and, at many centres, X-ray facilities
Primary Health Centres
Outpatient consultation for common illnesses, minor injuries, and chronic disease follow-up
Antenatal, natal, and postnatal care, including normal deliveries at 24x7 PHCs
Immunization, family planning services, and national health programme delivery (TB, malaria, non-communicable disease screening, and similar)
Basic laboratory tests (blood, urine, blood sugar, malaria rapid tests, and similar)
First-level stabilization and referral of serious cases to a CHC or the District Headquarters Hospital
How to Reach Them (General Guidance)
Since exact addresses and phone numbers are not being invented here, the following general approaches can help locate and reach the correct facility:
Ask the local ASHA worker, ANM, or Anganwadi worker — they know the nearest Sub-Centre and PHC serving a household and can help with referral upward if needed.

Every block headquarters in Cuttack district has a CHC; the block administrative (Block Development/Tahasil) office can confirm its exact location. The Cuttack district administration's official website and the CDMO Cuttack office maintain listings of health facilities; these should be treated as the authoritative source for confirmed addresses and phone numbers. The National Health Mission (NHM) Odisha and Odisha Directorate of Health Services websites publish facility directories and health scheme information at the state level. The 108 (emergency response) and 102 (patient transport / maternal-child) ambulance services can be used to reach an appropriate facility in an emergency, and can also help route a patient to the correct level of care.

For the District Headquarters Hospital specifically, and to distinguish it from SCB Medical College and Hospital in the same city, confirm the current address and scope of services with the district health administration before travelling.

When to Go to District Hospital vs PHC
Go to a PHC (or Sub-Centre) first for:
Routine illnesses — fever, cold, minor infections, common ailments
Antenatal check-ups, immunizations, and family planning services
Normal, uncomplicated deliveries at a 24x7-designated PHC
Basic diagnostic tests and follow-up for chronic conditions already under management
Minor injuries and first-aid level care
Go to (or be referred to) a CHC for:
Cases needing minor surgery, specialist consultation, or inpatient observation beyond what a PHC can provide
Complicated deliveries or emergency obstetric care, especially at an FRU-designated CHC
Situations where the PHC has stabilized a patient but recommended referral
Go directly to the District Headquarters Hospital for:
Serious emergencies — major trauma, accidents, severe medical emergencies where higher-level care is clearly needed
Conditions requiring specialist care, surgery, or diagnostics not available at PHC or CHC level
Cases already referred by a PHC or CHC as needing secondary-level hospital care
Situations covered under empanelled schemes (e.g., PM-JAY) requiring hospital-level admission — confirm current scheme coverage locally
As a general rule, the public health system is designed as a step-up referral chain: Sub-Centre → PHC → CHC → District Headquarters Hospital → Medical College Hospital, with each level equipped for progressively more complex care.

In Cuttack's case, the presence of SCB Medical College and Hospital in the same city as the DHH means very serious or specialized cases may ultimately be referred there, but the DHH and CHCs remain the intended first stops for most secondary-level care under the standard referral pathway. Bypassing lower tiers is appropriate mainly in genuine emergencies, where reaching the nearest capable facility quickly — often via 108 ambulance services — matters more than following the tier order.

Dengue Fever: Public Health Awareness Guide
A simple reference for community health awareness (for use by health awareness chatbots and community health workers)
Overview
Dengue fever is an illness spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It is caused by the dengue virus and is common in tropical and sub-tropical parts of the world, including most of India. Both children and adults can get dengue. Many people who get infected have no symptoms at all or only mild symptoms, and most people recover fully within one to two weeks with proper rest and care. In a small number of cases, dengue can become severe and needs urgent hospital treatment.

In a small number of cases, dengue can become severe and needs urgent hospital treatment. Because there is no specific medicine that cures dengue, the best protection is preventing mosquito bites and stopping mosquitoes from breeding around homes and villages. Common Symptoms
Dengue usually begins suddenly, about four to seven days after the mosquito bite. Common signs include:
Sudden high fever
Severe headache, often with pain behind the eyes
Muscle, joint, and body pain (sometimes called “break-bone fever”)
Nausea and vomiting
Skin rash, which may appear a few days after the fever starts
Weakness and loss of appetite
Mild bleeding, such as from the gums or nose, in some cases
Most people start feeling better after the fever comes down, usually within a week.

However, a few people can develop severe dengue just as the fever is going down, which is why it is important to keep watching for warning signs even after the fever reduces. Causes
Dengue is caused by the dengue virus, which spreads to people through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. These mosquitoes are most active during the day, especially in the early morning and before sunset. They breed in clean, standing water that collects in and around homes, such as in water storage containers, discarded tyres, flower pots, coolers, tanks, tins, and other containers that hold rainwater. Dengue does not spread directly from one person to another through touch, coughing, or sharing food; it spreads only through mosquito bites.

A person can get dengue more than once in their life, and a second infection can sometimes be more severe than the first. When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs – Act Immediately)
Most dengue cases can be managed at home with rest and fluids, but some warning signs mean the person needs urgent medical attention, ideally at a hospital or health centre.

Go to a doctor or hospital immediately if the person has any of the following:
Severe stomach pain or continuous vomiting
Bleeding from the nose, gums, or blood in vomit or stool (black stool)
Difficulty breathing or fast, shallow breathing
Extreme tiredness, restlessness, or confusion
Cold, clammy skin or pale skin
Not passing urine for several hours
Fever that suddenly drops but the person feels worse, not better
Any bleeding under the skin (small red or purple spots)
These warning signs often appear as the fever is coming down, usually three to seven days after symptoms start.

Infants, pregnant women, older adults, and people with other health conditions should be watched extra carefully and taken to a doctor early, even for mild symptoms, since they have a higher chance of complications.

Home Care and Prevention
Home care (for mild dengue without warning signs):
Rest as much as possible and avoid heavy physical activity
Drink plenty of fluids – water, oral rehydration solution (ORS), coconut water, or fruit juice – to prevent dehydration
Eat light, easily digestible food
Check body temperature regularly and watch for warning signs
Do not take any medicine without consulting a doctor, since some common painkillers can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue
Use a mosquito net or repellent while resting, so the patient does not spread infection to more mosquitoes, which can then bite others
Prevention (stopping mosquito breeding):
Empty, clean, or cover all containers that can collect water – buckets, drums, coolers, flower pots, and tanks – at least once a week
Remove stagnant water from around the house, including in tyres, broken pots, and construction sites
Keep drains clear and avoid letting water collect in open spaces
Use mosquito nets, screens on windows, and mosquito repellents, especially during the day
Wear clothes that cover arms and legs, particularly for children and during outdoor work
Support community and municipal efforts such as fogging and larvicide spraying, and report breeding sites to local health workers
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, dengue follows a clear seasonal pattern linked to the state's monsoon and post-monsoon periods.

Cases typically begin rising with the arrival of the south-west monsoon around June to July and peak during the post-monsoon months of September to November, when heavy rainfall combined with warm, humid weather creates ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes. Coastal and urban districts, including areas around Bhubaneswar, Cuttack, Khurda, and Jajpur, along with parts of southern and tribal-dominated districts, have historically reported higher case numbers during these months, though outbreaks can occur across most districts of the state. Because Odisha experiences heavy monsoon rainfall and frequent waterlogging, extra care is needed to prevent water from collecting in open drains, construction sites, discarded containers, tyres, and low-lying areas after rains.

Rural households should regularly check water storage pots, coolers, and any containers used for rainwater harvesting, since these become common breeding grounds once the rains begin. Community-level cleanliness drives, timely desilting of drains, and prompt reporting of fever cases to the nearest health centre or Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) worker can help control local outbreaks. Awareness and early action before and during the monsoon season are especially important in reducing the annual rise in dengue cases seen across the state.

Understanding Diabetes
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Diabetes is a long-term health condition that affects how the body turns food into energy. Normally, the food we eat is broken down into sugar (glucose), which enters the blood. A hormone called insulin, made by the pancreas, helps this sugar move into the body's cells to be used for energy. In diabetes, the body either does not make enough insulin, or is unable to use the insulin it makes properly. As a result, sugar builds up in the blood instead of reaching the cells. Over time, this extra sugar in the blood can damage the heart, eyes, kidneys, nerves, and blood vessels.

Diabetes is one of the most common long-term health conditions in India today, affecting both cities and villages. It can affect adults and, increasingly, younger people as well. The good news is that with awareness, healthy habits, and regular check-ups, diabetes can often be prevented, or managed well if it does occur. Common Symptoms
Diabetes often develops slowly, and many people do not notice any symptoms in the early stages.

When symptoms do appear, they may include:
Feeling very thirsty often, even after drinking water
Passing urine more often than usual, including at night
Feeling unusually tired or weak
Losing weight without trying
Feeling hungry more often than normal
Blurred or unclear eyesight
Cuts, wounds, or sores that take longer than usual to heal
Frequent infections, such as skin or urinary infections
Tingling, numbness, or a burning feeling in the hands or feet
Because these symptoms can be mild at first, many people are not aware they have diabetes until it is checked through a simple blood test.

Causes
Diabetes can develop for several reasons, and often more than one factor is involved:
Family history – having parents or close relatives with diabetes increases risk
Being overweight or having extra fat around the stomach
Low levels of physical activity or a sedentary daily routine
Unhealthy eating habits, such as regularly eating a lot of sugar, refined (polished) grains, oily, or fried food
Increasing age, especially after 40 years
High blood pressure or high cholesterol
Diabetes that occurs during pregnancy (gestational diabetes), which can raise future risk for both mother and child
Long-term stress and irregular sleep patterns
In some cases, particularly in younger people, diabetes occurs because the body's immune system affects the pancreas directly.

This form is not linked to lifestyle and cannot currently be prevented, but it can still be managed well with proper medical care. When to See a Doctor
Anyone experiencing the common symptoms above should visit the nearest health centre or doctor for a simple blood sugar test.

In addition, the following signs need urgent medical attention and should never be ignored:
Severe weakness, confusion, difficulty staying awake, or fainting
Fast breathing, breathlessness, or a fruity smell in the breath
Repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down
Severe stomach pain
A wound, ulcer, or sore (especially on the foot) that is not healing, is swollen, or has pus
Sudden blurred vision or loss of vision
Chest pain, pressure, or discomfort
Numbness, weakness, or slurred speech on one side of the body
Signs of very low blood sugar in a known diabetic person, such as sudden sweating, shakiness, or dizziness that does not improve after eating something sweet
Diabetes discovered or suspected during pregnancy
If any of these red-flag signs appear, the person should be taken to the nearest hospital or Primary Health Centre (PHC) immediately.

Early action can prevent serious complications and save lives. Home Care and Prevention
Many cases of the common (type 2) form of diabetes can be prevented or delayed through simple, everyday lifestyle habits.

These same habits also help people already living with diabetes stay healthier:
Healthy Eating
Include more vegetables, leafy greens, whole grains (such as unpolished rice, ragi, or millets), and pulses in daily meals
Reduce sugar, sweets, cold drinks, and refined white rice or maida-based foods
Limit deep-fried and oily food; choose boiled, steamed, or lightly cooked options when possible
Eat meals at regular times and avoid skipping meals, especially breakfast
Drink plenty of plain water through the day
Staying Active
Aim for at least 30 minutes of walking or physical activity most days of the week
Simple daily activities like farm work, walking to the market, or household chores also help
Avoid sitting for very long periods without moving
Healthy Body Weight and Habits
Maintaining a healthy body weight lowers the risk of developing diabetes
Avoid tobacco (smoking or chewing) and limit alcohol, as both increase risk
Get adequate sleep and try to manage stress through rest, family support, or community activities
General Care Awareness
Get blood sugar checked regularly, especially after age 40 or if there is a family history of diabetes
Check feet regularly for cuts, blisters, or wounds, and keep them clean and protected
Attend follow-up check-ups at the local health centre as advised
Always take rest and fluids when unwell, and consult a doctor rather than self-treating
This document does not cover medicines or treatment plans.

Any decisions about medication, dosage, or treatment must be made only by a qualified doctor. Odisha-Specific Notes
Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes are a growing health concern across Odisha, in both urban and rural areas. Awareness and early detection remain especially important in rural and tribal regions, where access to regular health check-ups can be limited.

Free screening for diabetes, blood pressure, and other common NCDs is available at government health facilities, including Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), and Community Health Centres (CHCs), under national and state NCD control programmes
Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres in Odisha offer screening, basic check-ups, and referral services for diabetes and related conditions
ASHA and Anganwadi workers in local communities can guide families toward the nearest screening centre and government health schemes
Traditional Odia diets rich in vegetables, pulses, and millets (such as mandia/ragi) can support healthy eating; reducing added sugar, refined rice portions, and fried snacks (such as pakoda or oily street food) is helpful for prevention
People in coastal, hilly, and tribal districts are encouraged to use local health camps and mobile medical units where available for regular check-ups
Residents are encouraged to visit their nearest government health facility for free or low-cost screening rather than waiting for symptoms to appear.

Diarrhoea and Dehydration in Children
A Public Health Awareness Reference
For community health awareness use • Simple language for rural readers
Overview
Diarrhoea means passing loose or watery stools three or more times in a day. It is one of the most common illnesses in young children and is a leading cause of child sickness and death in many parts of India, including rural and tribal areas. The main danger from diarrhoea is not the loose motions themselves, but the loss of water and salts from the body, known as dehydration. Dehydration can become severe within hours, especially in small children and infants, and can be life-threatening if not treated in time.

The good news is that most cases of diarrhoea can be safely managed at home with simple fluids, continued feeding, and Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), along with quick recognition of warning signs that need medical care. Common Symptoms
Diarrhoea and dehydration can show up in different ways.

Common Symptoms
Diarrhoea and dehydration can show up in different ways. Common signs include:
Frequent loose or watery stools
Stomach pain or cramps
Nausea or vomiting
Mild fever
Weakness or tiredness
Loss of appetite
Signs that the body is losing too much fluid (early dehydration) include:
Thirst, dry mouth, or dry lips
Fewer wet diapers, or passing less urine than usual
Dark yellow urine
Reduced activity, irritability, or crying without tears
Sunken eyes
In infants, a sunken soft spot on the top of the head
Causes
Diarrhoea in children is usually caused by infections that spread through unsafe water, unwashed hands, or contaminated food.

Common causes include:
Viral infections (such as rotavirus), which are the most common cause in young children
Bacterial infections from contaminated food or water
Parasites and worms, especially where sanitation is poor
Drinking unclean or unboiled water
Poor handwashing, especially before eating and after using the toilet
Unsafe food storage or spoiled food
Malnutrition, which makes children more vulnerable to infection and to severe dehydration
When to See a Doctor — Red Flag Signs
Most diarrhoea can be managed at home, but the caregiver should take the child to the nearest health centre, ASHA worker, or hospital immediately if any of the following are seen:
Blood in the stool
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep down fluids or ORS
Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry mouth, no tears, little or no urine for 6 hours or more
Child is unusually sleepy, difficult to wake, or unresponsive
High fever that does not settle
Diarrhoea continues for more than 2 days without improvement
Severe stomach pain
Signs of severe weakness, fits (convulsions), or the child cannot drink or breastfeed at all
Infant below 6 months of age with diarrhoea
Child is malnourished or has an existing serious illness
If any of these signs appear, do not wait — seek medical help immediately.

ORS should still be given on the way to the health facility, if the child is able to drink. Home Care and Prevention
Home care during diarrhoea
Give ORS after every loose stool to replace lost fluids and salts. Continue breastfeeding infants — do not stop breastfeeding during diarrhoea. Continue feeding the child age-appropriate food; do not withhold food. Small, frequent meals are best. Give plenty of clean fluids such as ORS, safe drinking water, and home fluids like rice water or diluted buttermilk. Let the child rest as needed. Wash hands with soap before feeding the child and after cleaning the child's stool. Do not give unnecessary medicines without consulting a health worker or doctor. Watch closely for the red-flag signs listed above.

Watch closely for the red-flag signs listed above. How to prepare ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) at home
If a ready-made ORS packet from a health centre or ASHA worker is available, always prefer that — just follow the instructions printed on the packet, mixing it with the exact amount of clean water stated. If a packet is not available, a simple home sugar-salt solution can be prepared:
Wash hands well with soap and clean water. Take 1 litre of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled, if the water source is not safe). Add 6 level teaspoons of sugar. Add half (1/2) a level teaspoon of salt. Stir well until the sugar and salt fully dissolve. Give small sips frequently using a clean cup or spoon — do not use a feeding bottle.

Give small sips frequently using a clean cup or spoon — do not use a feeding bottle. If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and then continue giving small sips more slowly. Prepare a fresh solution every day; discard any solution left over after 24 hours. General guide for how much ORS to give after each loose stool: children under 2 years — about a quarter to half a cup; children 2 to 10 years — about half to one cup; older children and adults — as much as they will comfortably drink. The exact amount is less important than giving fluids often, in small sips, and continuing until the diarrhoea stops. Prevention
Drink and use only clean, safe drinking water; boil water if the source is uncertain. Wash hands with soap at key times: before eating, before feeding a child, and after using the toilet.

Use a toilet/latrine and avoid open defecation. Keep food covered and eat freshly cooked food; avoid stale or exposed food. Wash fruits and vegetables before eating. Ensure children complete their scheduled vaccinations, including the rotavirus vaccine given under the national immunisation programme. Keep the child's surroundings and drinking water storage containers clean. Continue exclusive breastfeeding for infants up to 6 months, as advised by health workers, as it protects against infections. Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, diarrhoeal disease remains a significant concern, particularly during the summer and monsoon months, and among children in rural, tribal, and flood-prone areas where safe water and sanitation access can be limited.

Families are encouraged to keep the following in mind:
Under the national Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight / STOP Diarrhoea Campaign, ASHA workers pre-position ORS packets in households with children under five years — ask your local ASHA or Anganwadi worker for ORS packets and guidance. ORS-Zinc corners are set up at health sub-centres, primary health centres, and Anganwadi centres during the campaign period; zinc supplements, along with ORS, help reduce the duration and severity of diarrhoea in children when advised by a health worker. During and after heavy rains or flooding, take extra care with drinking water — use only boiled, chlorinated, or otherwise treated water, as flood conditions increase the risk of contaminated water sources.

Contact your nearest Sub-Centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), Community Health Centre (CHC), ASHA, or ANM promptly if a child shows any red-flag sign, or call the Odisha health helpline / 108 ambulance service in an emergency. Participate in local awareness activities on hygiene, safe water, and sanitation conducted by the Odisha Health and Family Welfare Department and the National Health Mission. Source Basis
