Elderly Health Awareness
Simple Steps for a Healthier, Safer Old Age
A Public Health Awareness Guide for Families and Communities
1. Overview
As people grow older, their bodies go through natural changes. Bones become weaker, eyesight and hearing may reduce, muscles lose strength, and the body takes longer to recover from illness. These changes are a normal part of ageing, but many problems linked to old age can be reduced or managed if families and elders themselves stay aware and take small precautions. India's elderly population is growing steadily every year. Health authorities have recognised that older adults need special attention because they often deal with more than one health condition at the same time, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, joint pain, or heart disease.

This guide explains, in simple language, the common health concerns of old age, how to prevent falls, and how to use medicines safely. It is meant for families in villages, small towns, and cities who want to care for their elders in the right way. 2. Key Practices
A. Common Age-Related Health Concerns
Joint and bone problems: Pain in knees, hips, and back is common due to weakening bones and joints. Regular gentle movement and a diet with calcium (milk, curd, green leafy vegetables) can help. High blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease: These are called non-communicable diseases and are very common in old age. Regular check-ups at the nearest sub-centre, PHC, or hospital help catch problems early. Weak eyesight and hearing: Cataracts and hearing loss increase with age.

Weak eyesight and hearing: Cataracts and hearing loss increase with age. Yearly eye and ear check-ups can prevent accidents and improve quality of life. Memory and mental health: Some elders may face memory loss, confusion, loneliness, or sadness. Family time, social activity, and talking openly about feelings are important. Weakness and poor nutrition: Loss of appetite and reduced ability to chew can lead to poor nutrition. Soft, nutritious, home-cooked food in small, frequent meals is helpful. B. Fall Prevention
Falls are one of the most common and serious risks for elderly people. A fall that seems minor can lead to a fracture, especially of the hip, and a long recovery. Most falls happen at home and can be prevented with simple changes.

Most falls happen at home and can be prevented with simple changes. Keep floors dry, clean, and free of loose wires, mats, or clutter, especially near the bathroom and stairs. Ensure good lighting in rooms, staircases, and passages, particularly at night. Fix strong handrails in bathrooms and along staircases; use a non-slip mat in the bathing area. Encourage the use of a walking stick or support if the elder feels unsteady while walking. Ask elders to rise slowly from sitting or lying down, as sudden movement can cause dizziness. Get eyesight, footwear, and blood pressure checked regularly, since poor vision, loose slippers, and low blood pressure are common causes of falls. C.

C. General Medication Safety Awareness
Older adults often take medicines for more than one condition, which increases the chance of mistakes or side effects. The following general practices support safe use of medicines, without replacing a doctor's or pharmacist's advice. Always take medicines exactly as prescribed by a qualified doctor; never start, stop, or change a dose on your own. Keep a simple written list or a medicine box with day and time markings to avoid missing or repeating a dose. Inform every doctor about all the medicines the elder is already taking, including any bought without prescription. Store medicines safely, away from direct sunlight and out of reach of children, and check expiry dates regularly.

Report any unusual symptoms after starting a new medicine, such as dizziness, drowsiness, or stomach upset, to a health worker or doctor promptly. Avoid sharing medicines between family members, as the same symptom can have different causes and treatments. 3. Why It Matters
Small, consistent efforts in elderly care can prevent big health emergencies. A fall that leads to a hip fracture, or a medicine taken incorrectly, can turn a healthy elder into someone dependent on others for months. On the other hand, regular check-ups, a safe home environment, and careful use of medicines allow elders to stay active, independent, and mentally well for longer. Caring for elderly family members is also a shared social responsibility.

Caring for elderly family members is also a shared social responsibility. When communities and families stay informed, elders feel respected and supported rather than isolated. This directly improves not just physical health but also emotional wellbeing in old age. 4. Odisha-Specific Context
The Government of Odisha, through the Department of Health and Family Welfare and the National Health Mission Odisha, implements the National Programme for the Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE). Under this programme, geriatric clinics and dedicated elderly care services are being expanded in district hospitals and community health centres across the state, and separate queues for elderly patients have been introduced in some OPDs to reduce waiting time.

Elders and families in Odisha, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, are encouraged to make use of nearby Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Bharat) for regular blood pressure, blood sugar, and general health screening, since these services are available close to home and are generally free of cost. Along with health services, central schemes such as the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme and assistive-device support under the Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana are also available to eligible senior citizens through local administration, and can ease the financial and physical burden of old age. 5. When to Seek Emergency Medical Care
Warning Signs That Should Never Be Treated at Home
A Public Safety Awareness Guide
This guide lists warning signs that always require IMMEDIATE medical attention. If you or someone near you has any of these symptoms, do not wait, do not try home remedies, and do not attempt to travel long distances alone. Go straight to the nearest hospital or emergency room, or call your local emergency ambulance number right away. Why This Matters
For certain symptoms, every minute counts. Conditions such as heart attack, stroke, severe bleeding, and meningitis can worsen very quickly, and the treatments that work best are often only effective if given early.

Waiting to "see if it gets better" can mean the difference between a full recovery and permanent damage, or between life and death. This guide is intentionally cautious: if a symptom is on this list, treat it as an emergency, even if the person seems to be coping or the symptom seems to be easing. Warning Signs That Need Immediate Care
1. Chest Pain or Pressure
Chest pain, tightness, pressure, or a squeezing sensation, especially if it spreads to the arm, jaw, neck, or back, or comes with sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath, can be a sign of a heart attack. Heart muscle can be permanently damaged within a short time if blood flow is blocked, so rapid treatment significantly improves the chance of survival and recovery.

Act now: Call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital immediately. Do not drive yourself if possible; do not wait to see if the pain passes. 2. Difficulty Breathing or Severe Shortness of Breath
Struggling to breathe, breathlessness that does not improve with rest, gasping for air, or lips or fingertips turning blue or grey are signs that the body is not getting enough oxygen. This can be caused by a severe asthma attack, a serious infection, a heart problem, a blocked airway, or a severe allergic reaction, all of which can become life-threatening within minutes. Act now: Call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital immediately. Sit the person upright if possible and loosen tight clothing while help is on the way. 3.

Sit the person upright if possible and loosen tight clothing while help is on the way. 3. Severe Bleeding
Bleeding that will not stop after applying firm, direct pressure for several minutes, bleeding that is spurting or gushing, or a large, deep wound can quickly lead to dangerous blood loss and shock. This includes severe bleeding after an accident, a deep cut, or heavy bleeding during or after pregnancy. Act now: Apply firm, continuous pressure with a clean cloth and call emergency services or get to the nearest hospital immediately. Do not remove an object stuck in a wound; keep pressure around it instead. 4.

Do not remove an object stuck in a wound; keep pressure around it instead. 4. Sudden Weakness, Numbness, or Signs of Stroke
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, a drooping face, slurred or confused speech, sudden vision problems, sudden severe headache, or loss of balance can be signs of a stroke. Brain cells begin to die within minutes when blood flow is interrupted, and treatments that can limit damage generally only work if given very soon after symptoms start. A simple way to check is the FAST test: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call for help. Act now: Call emergency services or get to the nearest hospital immediately, even if the symptoms seem to improve or come and go. Note the time the symptoms started, as this helps doctors decide on treatment. 5.

Note the time the symptoms started, as this helps doctors decide on treatment. 5. High Fever With a Stiff Neck
A high fever combined with a stiff neck, severe headache, sensitivity to light, confusion, or a rash that does not fade when pressed can be signs of meningitis or a similar severe infection affecting the brain and spinal cord. This condition can worsen very rapidly and can be fatal or cause lasting harm without urgent treatment, particularly in young children, older adults, and people with weaker immune systems. Act now: Go to the nearest hospital or call emergency services immediately. Do not wait to see if the fever comes down on its own. 6.

Do not wait to see if the fever comes down on its own. 6. Severe Abdominal Pain
Sudden, severe, or worsening pain in the abdomen, especially if it is constant, focused in one area, or comes with vomiting, fever, a rigid or very tender belly, or blood in vomit or stool, can indicate a serious internal problem such as appendicitis, a perforated organ, a blocked intestine, or internal bleeding. In pregnant women, severe abdominal pain can also signal a serious pregnancy-related complication. Act now: Go to the nearest hospital or call emergency services immediately. Avoid eating, drinking, or taking pain medicine until a doctor has assessed the situation, as this can make diagnosis more difficult. 7.

7. Loss of Consciousness
Fainting that does not resolve quickly, being unresponsive to voice or touch, or any period where a person cannot be woken up are medical emergencies. Loss of consciousness can be caused by a heart problem, a severe drop in blood sugar, a stroke, a serious head injury, severe blood loss, or a seizure, several of which require urgent treatment to prevent permanent harm. Act now: Call emergency services immediately. While waiting for help, keep the person lying on their side if they are breathing, and do not put anything in their mouth. General Safety Reminders
Do not wait for symptoms to "get worse" before seeking help; for the conditions listed above, acting early gives the best chance of a full recovery.

Do not rely on home remedies, rest, or over-the-counter medicine alone when any of these warning signs are present. If you are unsure whether a situation is a true emergency, it is safer to seek immediate medical care than to wait and assume it will pass. Keep the nearest hospital's location and your local emergency ambulance number easily accessible for yourself and your family. Daily Hygiene, Safe Water, and Sanitation
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Good hygiene, safe drinking water, and proper sanitation are among the simplest and most powerful ways to protect health. Many common illnesses, especially diarrhoea, typhoid, cholera, worm infections, and skin and eye infections, spread because of dirty hands, unsafe water, or poor sanitation. These illnesses are largely preventable. Simple daily habits, such as washing hands at the right times, drinking clean water, and using a toilet instead of open defecation, can greatly reduce sickness in a household and community.

Good hygiene is especially important for protecting young children, pregnant women, and elderly family members, who are more vulnerable to infections. This document explains the key daily practices that support health, why they matter, and how government programmes are helping communities in Odisha and across India access safe water and sanitation.

Key Practices
Handwashing
Wash hands with soap and clean water before eating or preparing food
Wash hands after using the toilet
Wash hands after cleaning a child, changing a baby, or handling waste
Wash hands before feeding a baby or young child
Rub soap on both sides of the hands, between fingers, and under nails for at least 20 seconds, then rinse with clean water
If soap is not available, ash or clean sand can be used, followed by rinsing with water
Safe Drinking Water
Drink water only from a safe, protected source, such as a treated tap connection, protected borewell, or covered well
Store drinking water in a clean, covered container, and use a clean cup or ladle to draw water rather than dipping hands inside
If the safety of water is uncertain, boil it before drinking, or use a household water filter or purification method recommended by local health workers
Keep drinking water separate from water used for washing or other household purposes
Clean water storage containers regularly to prevent contamination
Sanitation
Always use a toilet instead of defecating in the open, for both adults and children
Keep toilets clean and in good repair, with water available for use after each visit
Dispose of household waste and garbage properly, away from drinking water sources
Keep the area around the home, especially around water sources, free from stagnant water and waste, as these attract mosquitoes and other disease-carrying insects
Wash fruits and vegetables with clean water before eating or cooking
Cover food to protect it from flies and dust
Why It Matters
Diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid, hepatitis A, and cholera spread mainly through dirty hands, contaminated water, and unsafe sanitation.

Washing hands with soap at key times can significantly reduce the spread of diarrhoeal and respiratory illnesses, both of which remain leading causes of sickness, especially in young children. Unsafe water and poor sanitation also contribute to worm infections, which can affect children's growth, nutrition, and school attendance. Skin infections and eye infections such as trachoma are also linked to poor hygiene and limited access to clean water. When communities have access to safe water, functioning toilets, and good hygiene habits, rates of illness fall, children stay healthier and attend school more regularly, and healthcare costs for families are reduced. Good hygiene during childbirth and in the days after also protects the health of mothers and newborns.

These simple practices are among the most cost-effective ways to protect community health, alongside vaccination and good nutrition. Odisha-Specific Context
Odisha has made significant progress in expanding access to sanitation and safe drinking water in recent years, supported by national and state-level programmes.

Under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin), launched by the Government of India, Odisha has worked to build household toilets and eliminate open defecation across its villages, with a large majority of villages in the state now recognised as Open Defecation Free (ODF) Plus
The Odisha Water and Sanitation Mission (OWSM) coordinates state efforts on rural drinking water supply and sanitation, working alongside the Panchayati Raj and Drinking Water Department
The Jal Jeevan Mission aims to provide piped drinking water connections to rural households across Odisha, improving access to safe water at the doorstep
Behaviour change campaigns, along with the efforts of ASHA and Anganwadi workers, continue to promote handwashing, toilet use, and safe water practices in rural and tribal communities
Community participation, including cleanliness drives and local sanitation committees, plays an important role in sustaining these gains at the village level
Residents are encouraged to make full use of local toilets, safe water connections, and hygiene facilities provided under these programmes, and to reach out to their nearest Anganwadi centre, ASHA worker, or Gram Panchayat office for support or repairs.

Understanding High Blood Pressure
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is a condition where the force of blood pushing against the walls of the blood vessels stays too high over time. Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120/80. The first (higher) number is the pressure when the heart beats, and the second (lower) number is the pressure when the heart rests between beats. A blood pressure reading of 140/90 or higher, checked on more than one occasion, is generally considered high.

Blood pressure naturally rises and falls during the day depending on activity, emotion, and rest, but when it stays high most of the time, it can slowly damage the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. High blood pressure is often called a 'silent' condition because most people do not feel unwell even when their blood pressure is high. It is very common across India, in both cities and villages, and its numbers are rising. The only reliable way to know if a person has high blood pressure is to get it checked with a blood pressure machine. Common Symptoms
Most people with high blood pressure do not notice any symptoms at all, which is why regular checking is so important.

When symptoms do appear, they are often signs that blood pressure has become very high, and may include:
Headache, especially at the back of the head
Dizziness or a spinning sensation
Blurred or disturbed eyesight
Chest discomfort or a feeling of heaviness
Shortness of breath
Nosebleeds that are unusual or hard to stop
A fast or irregular heartbeat
Unusual tiredness or fatigue
Since high blood pressure usually has no warning signs, it is often found only during a routine health check. Regular blood pressure checks, even when a person feels completely well, are the best way to detect it early.

Causes
High blood pressure often develops because of a combination of habits, body factors, and family background:
Eating too much salt, or regularly eating salty, packaged, or pickled foods
Low intake of fruits and vegetables
Being overweight or having extra fat around the stomach
Low levels of physical activity
Use of tobacco (smoking or chewing) and regular alcohol use
Long-term stress and poor sleep
Family history of high blood pressure
Increasing age, especially after 40 years
Existing health conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease
Exposure to air pollution over long periods
In most people, several of these factors act together over time. This is why lifestyle habits play such a large role in both preventing and managing high blood pressure.

When to See a Doctor
Every adult should get their blood pressure checked regularly, even without any symptoms, since high blood pressure often has no warning signs.

In addition, the following signs point to a possible emergency and need urgent medical attention without delay:
Severe headache that comes on suddenly and does not go away
Chest pain, tightness, or pressure
Difficulty breathing or severe shortness of breath
Sudden weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of the face or body
Slurred speech or trouble speaking or understanding others
Sudden blurred vision, double vision, or loss of vision
Confusion, difficulty staying awake, or fainting
Severe nosebleed that will not stop
Very high blood pressure reading along with any of the above symptoms
High blood pressure discovered or suspected during pregnancy, especially with swelling of hands or face
If any of these red-flag signs appear, the person should be taken to the nearest hospital or Primary Health Centre (PHC) immediately, as they could indicate a heart attack, stroke, or other emergency.

Every hour matters in these situations. Home Care and Prevention
High blood pressure can often be prevented or kept under control through simple, everyday lifestyle habits.

These habits also support people already living with high blood pressure:
Healthy Eating
Reduce salt intake; avoid adding extra salt at the table and limit pickles, papad, and salty snacks
Eat more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains such as unpolished rice or millets
Limit fried, oily, and processed packaged foods
Choose fresh, home-cooked food over ready-made or restaurant food when possible
Drink enough water through the day
Staying Active
Aim for at least 30 minutes of walking or moderate physical activity most days of the week
Everyday activities such as farm work, walking, or household chores also help
Avoid long periods of sitting without moving
Healthy Habits
Maintain a healthy body weight
Avoid tobacco in all forms and limit alcohol consumption
Manage stress through rest, family time, prayer, or community activities
Aim for regular, adequate sleep each night
General Care Awareness
Get blood pressure checked regularly, especially after age 40 or with a family history of hypertension
Keep a simple record of blood pressure readings if checked often
Attend follow-up check-ups at the local health centre as advised
If feeling unwell, rest, drink fluids, and consult a doctor rather than self-treating
This document does not cover medicines or treatment plans.

Any decisions about medication, dosage, or treatment must be made only by a qualified doctor. Odisha-Specific Notes
High blood pressure is a growing health concern across Odisha, affecting people in both urban and rural areas. Because it usually has no symptoms, many people in the state are unaware they have it until a check-up or an emergency reveals it.

Free blood pressure screening is available at government health facilities, including Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), and Community Health Centres (CHCs), under national and state NCD control programmes

ASHA and Anganwadi workers can help families identify the nearest screening centre and connect with government health schemes
Traditional Odia cooking often uses generous amounts of salt and oil; gradually reducing salt in daily cooking and limiting fried snacks like pakoda supports healthy blood pressure

Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY)
India's Maternal Health Cash Assistance Scheme, Explained Simply
A Public Awareness Reference Guide
1. Overview
Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a safe motherhood scheme run by the Government of India under the National Health Mission (NHM). It was launched in April 2005 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The scheme's main goal is to reduce deaths of mothers and newborns by encouraging pregnant women to deliver their babies in a hospital or health centre, with the help of trained doctors and nurses, instead of at home without medical support. JSY does this by providing cash assistance directly to the mother when she delivers at a government hospital or an accredited private health facility.

It also involves ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) workers, who guide and support pregnant women through pregnancy check-ups, the delivery itself, and care afterward. JSY is implemented in every state and union territory, with extra focus on states that have historically had lower rates of hospital deliveries, known as Low Performing States (LPS). 2. Eligibility
Eligibility under JSY depends partly on where a woman lives and, in some cases, on her economic background:
In Low Performing States, all pregnant women delivering in a government or accredited private health facility are eligible for cash assistance, regardless of their age or how many children they already have.

In High Performing States, women from Below Poverty Line (BPL) households, and women belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC) or Scheduled Tribes (ST), are eligible for cash assistance for institutional delivery, generally up to two live births. BPL pregnant women who prefer to deliver at home, rather than at a health facility, are also entitled to a smaller cash assistance, regardless of age or number of children. Women choosing to deliver at an accredited private hospital are usually required to show valid BPL, SC, or ST proof, along with a referral from the ASHA worker, ANM, or medical officer.

Because eligibility rules can vary slightly depending on the state's classification and local guidelines, pregnant women and their families should confirm current criteria with their nearest ASHA worker, ANM, or health centre. 3. Benefits
JSY combines a cash incentive with supportive care during pregnancy, delivery, and after childbirth:
Cash Assistance for Institutional Delivery
* Low Performing States generally include states that have historically had lower institutional delivery rates; all other states and union territories are classified as High Performing States. Actual classification and amounts may be revised over time. Other Benefits
A separate incentive is paid to the ASHA worker for accompanying and supporting the mother through antenatal check-ups and institutional delivery.

At least a minimum number of free antenatal check-ups are provided before delivery, along with a Mother and Child Protection Card and a JSY card to track entitlements. JSY is closely linked with the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), which provides free delivery, free medicines, free diagnostic tests, free diet during the hospital stay, and free transport to and from the health facility, at no cost to the mother. Cash assistance is generally transferred directly into the mother's bank account, so beneficiaries are encouraged to open a bank account, including through schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, if they do not already have one. 4.

4. How to Apply
As soon as pregnancy is confirmed, register with the nearest Anganwadi Centre, Sub-Centre, or Primary Health Centre (PHC), ideally within the first few months. The local ASHA worker can help with this registration. Complete the recommended antenatal check-ups and collect the Mother and Child Protection Card and JSY card issued by the ANM or ASHA worker; these track eligibility and entitlements through the pregnancy. Provide bank account details and required identity documents, such as Aadhaar, so that the cash assistance can be transferred directly once the delivery is complete. At the time of delivery, go to a government health facility or an accredited private hospital; the ASHA worker can help arrange transport and accompany the mother.

After delivery, ensure discharge documents and the JSY card are submitted at the health facility so that the cash assistance can be processed and credited to the bank account. Families without easy access to these facilities, or with questions about their entitlement, can reach out to their ASHA worker, the nearest PHC or Sub-Centre, or call the NHM toll-free health helpline for guidance. 5. Jaundice (Hepatitis A and E): A Public Health Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base
Overview
Jaundice is not a disease by itself. It is a sign that shows up when the liver is not working properly, causing the skin and the white part of the eyes to turn yellow. In India, one of the most common causes of sudden jaundice, especially in children and young adults, is a viral infection of the liver called hepatitis. Hepatitis A and hepatitis E are two types of liver infection that spread mainly through dirty water or contaminated food. Both illnesses are usually short-term and most people recover fully with rest and care at home. However, in some cases, especially in pregnant women, hepatitis E can become serious and needs urgent medical attention.

Because these infections spread easily in areas with unsafe drinking water and poor sanitation, they are common in many rural and semi-urban parts of India, including Odisha. Common Symptoms
Symptoms usually appear a few weeks after a person is exposed to the virus. Not everyone shows every symptom, and young children may have very mild or no symptoms at all. Common signs include:
Yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice)
Dark-coloured urine and pale or clay-coloured stools
Tiredness and weakness
Loss of appetite
Nausea and vomiting
Mild fever
Pain or discomfort in the upper right side of the stomach, near the liver
Joint pain (in some cases)
Most people feel unwell for one to a few weeks, and the illness usually goes away on its own within a few weeks to a couple of months.

Causes
Hepatitis A and hepatitis E viruses spread mainly through the faecal-oral route. This means the virus leaves the body of an infected person through stool and enters another person's body through the mouth, usually because of unsafe water or food. Common causes include:
Drinking water that has been contaminated with sewage or human waste
Eating food that was washed, cooked, or handled with unclean water or unwashed hands
Eating raw or undercooked food, including fruits and vegetables washed in unsafe water
Poor toilet and sanitation facilities that allow waste to mix with water sources
Living in crowded conditions with poor hygiene practices
These viruses are not usually spread by casual contact such as talking, hugging, or sitting near an infected person.

The main route of spread is through what people eat and drink. When to See a Doctor (Red Flags)
While most cases of hepatitis A and E are mild, some signs mean the illness may be getting serious and need urgent medical attention.

A doctor or health centre should be consulted immediately if a person has:
Yellowing of the eyes or skin that is getting worse quickly
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep fluids down
Severe weakness, confusion, or unusual drowsiness
Little or no urine, or urine that is very dark
Swelling of the stomach, legs, or feet
Bleeding or unusual bruising from the gums, nose, or skin
High fever that does not go down
Severe pain in the upper stomach
Any jaundice symptom in a pregnant woman, at any stage of pregnancy
Jaundice in a small child, an elderly person, or someone with an existing liver illness
Pregnant women need extra caution. Hepatitis E can be dangerous during pregnancy, particularly in the later months, and can lead to serious complications for both mother and baby.
Any pregnant woman with jaundice symptoms should be taken to a health facility without delay.

Any pregnant woman with jaundice symptoms should be taken to a health facility without delay. Home Care and Prevention
General care during recovery
Take plenty of rest and avoid heavy physical work until fully recovered
Drink enough clean, safe fluids to avoid dehydration
Eat light, easily digestible meals; avoid oily and heavy food
Avoid alcohol completely, as it puts extra strain on the liver
Do not take any medicine without a doctor's advice, since some medicines can affect the liver
Follow up with a health worker or doctor to check on recovery
Preventing hepatitis A and E
Drink only boiled, filtered, or otherwise safely treated water
Wash hands with soap and water before eating, before cooking, and after using the toilet
Use a clean toilet and avoid open defecation
Wash fruits and vegetables properly with safe water before eating
Eat freshly cooked, hot food and avoid food from unhygienic sources
Keep drinking water storage containers covered and clean
Ask a doctor or local health worker about the hepatitis A vaccine, especially for children
Community-level steps, such as protecting water sources from sewage contamination and improving sanitation, play a major role in preventing outbreaks.

Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha has seen repeated outbreaks of jaundice linked to hepatitis A and E, and unsafe drinking water has consistently been identified as the main cause. A well-documented outbreak in Sambalpur district and nearby areas involved thousands of cases and several deaths, traced back to contamination of the public water supply. Investigations into other outbreaks in the state, including in Bhubaneswar, have found that bore wells located near open sewage or drains were the source of infection. Studies of rural Odisha villages have also found frequent faecal contamination of ponds, groundwater sources, and stored household water, particularly during and after the monsoon season.

For rural communities in Odisha, the following points are especially important:
Flooding and heavy monsoon rains can contaminate wells, ponds, and pipelines, so extra care with water safety is needed during and after the rainy season
Water pipelines that run close to drains or sewage lines are a known risk; leaking or damaged pipes should be reported to local authorities
Bore wells and hand pumps near open defecation areas or soak pits should be avoided for drinking water where possible
Boiling water or using safe household treatment (such as proper chlorination or filtration) before drinking is strongly advised in areas without a reliable safe piped supply
Any sudden increase in jaundice cases in a village or locality should be reported promptly to the nearest health sub-centre or Anganwadi worker, as early reporting helps contain outbreaks
Government programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission aim to provide safe piped drinking water to rural households, and community participation in maintaining clean water sources remains an important part of preventing hepatitis outbreaks in the state.

Public Healthcare Facilities in Khordha District, Odisha
A Structured Reference Guide to District, Community, and Primary Health Facilities
Overview
Khordha district, home to the state capital Bhubaneswar, is served by a tiered public healthcare network run under the Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare and coordinated locally by the Chief District Medical Officer (CDMO), Khordha. The system follows the standard national structure used across India, which organizes facilities by population coverage and level of care — from village-level Sub-Centres up through Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and finally the District Headquarters Hospital (DHH), which acts as the district's main secondary-level referral point.

This structure is set out in the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) through the National Health Mission (NHM) and most recently revised in 2022. Facility Types
District Headquarters Hospital (DHH), Khordha
The DHH Khordha is the district's principal referral hospital. It originated as a sub-divisional hospital in 1975 and was formally designated the District Headquarters Hospital in 1994, after Khordha was carved out as a separate district. It functions as the top of the referral chain within the district, receiving cases referred from CHCs, PHCs, and Sub-Centres across all blocks.

Community Health Centres (CHCs)
CHCs are block-level referral units, typically built to serve a population of roughly 80,000 to 120,000 people depending on whether the area is a plain, hilly, or tribal region. Khordha district has multiple CHCs distributed across its blocks (for example, the CHC at Bhagabanpur Sasan serves the Balianta/Haladia area). A CHC is meant to have around 30 inpatient beds, an operation theatre, basic diagnostic and blood storage facilities, and specialist coverage in areas such as medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynaecology, and paediatrics, though the extent of specialist availability varies by centre. Some CHCs are additionally designated First Referral Units (FRUs) if they are equipped for round-the-clock emergency obstetric and newborn care.

Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
PHCs are the first point of contact with a qualified doctor for most rural and semi-urban residents, generally covering a population of around 20,000 to 30,000. Each PHC oversees a cluster of Sub-Centres in its area and is expected to provide outpatient consultation, a small number of inpatient beds (around four to six), basic laboratory testing, and normal delivery services where 24x7 delivery care has been designated. PHCs also supervise ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) and ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwife) workers operating at the village level.

Sub-Centres and Health & Wellness Centres
Below the PHC level, Health Sub-Centres — increasingly upgraded as Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) — are the most peripheral public health facilities, generally staffed by an ANM and a Community Health Officer. They focus on preventive and promotive care such as immunization, antenatal check-ups, and basic screening, and refer more complex cases upward to the PHC.

What Each Facility Handles
District Headquarters Hospital
Complex and emergency cases referred from CHCs and PHCs across the district
Wider range of specialist consultations and surgical services than block-level facilities
Diagnostics, blood storage/blood bank services, and inpatient care with larger bed capacity
Empanelment under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat–PM-JAY for cashless treatment (verify current empanelment status locally)
Serves as the secondary-level referral hospital for the entire district before onward referral to a medical college hospital, if needed
Community Health Centres
Referral care for PHCs within the block, plus specialist consultations for patients approaching directly
Inpatient care (around 30 beds), minor and some major surgical procedures, and operation theatre services
Emergency obstetric care and institutional deliveries, particularly at centres designated as First Referral Units
Basic diagnostics including laboratory and, at many centres, X-ray services
Primary Health Centres
Outpatient consultation for common illnesses, minor injuries, and chronic disease follow-up
Antenatal, natal, and postnatal care, including normal deliveries at 24x7 PHCs
Immunization, family planning services, and national health programme delivery (TB, malaria, non-communicable disease screening, etc.)
Basic laboratory tests (blood, urine, blood sugar, malaria rapid tests, and similar)
First-level stabilization and referral of serious cases to a CHC or the District Headquarters Hospital
How to Reach Them (General Guidance)
Because exact addresses and phone numbers are not being invented in this document, use the following general approaches to locate and reach the correct facility:
Ask the local ASHA worker, ANM, or Anganwadi worker — they know the nearest Sub-Centre and PHC serving a household and can guide referral upward if needed.

Every block headquarters in Khordha district has a CHC; the block administrative office can confirm its exact location. The Khordha district administration's official website and the CDMO Khordha office maintain listings of health facilities; these should be the source for confirmed addresses and phone numbers. The National Health Mission (NHM) Odisha and Odisha Directorate of Health Services websites publish facility directories and health scheme information at the state level. The 108 (emergency response) and 102 (patient transport/maternal-child) ambulance services can be used to reach an appropriate facility in an emergency, and can also help route a patient to the correct level of care.

For the District Headquarters Hospital specifically, it is located in Khordha town; the district administration office or DHH's own listing under the district health department should be used to confirm the current address before travelling.

When to Go to District Hospital vs PHC
Go to a PHC (or Sub-Centre) first for:
Routine illnesses — fever, cold, minor infections, common ailments
Antenatal check-ups, immunizations, and family planning services
Normal, uncomplicated deliveries at a 24x7-designated PHC
Basic diagnostic tests and follow-up for chronic conditions already under management
Minor injuries and first-aid level care
Go to (or be referred to) a CHC for:
Cases needing minor surgery, specialist consultation, or inpatient observation beyond what a PHC can provide
Complicated deliveries or emergency obstetric care, especially at an FRU-designated CHC
Situations where the PHC has stabilized a patient but recommended referral
Go directly to the District Headquarters Hospital for:
Serious emergencies — major trauma, accidents, severe medical emergencies where higher-level care is clearly needed
Conditions requiring specialist care, surgery, or diagnostics not available at PHC or CHC level
Cases already referred by a PHC or CHC as needing secondary-level hospital care
Situations covered under empanelled schemes (e.g., PM-JAY) requiring hospital-level admission — confirm current scheme coverage locally
As a general rule, the public health system is designed as a step-up referral chain: Sub-Centre → PHC → CHC → District Headquarters Hospital → Medical College Hospital, with each level equipped for progressively more complex care.

Bypassing lower tiers is appropriate mainly in genuine emergencies, where reaching the nearest capable facility quickly — often via 108 ambulance services — matters more than following the tier order.

Malaria: Public Health Awareness Guide
A simple reference for community health awareness (for use by health awareness chatbots and community health workers)
Overview
Malaria is a serious illness spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It is caused by a tiny parasite, not by a virus or bacteria, and it does not spread from one person to another through touch or air. Malaria is common in many warm, tropical parts of the world, including large parts of India, and it can affect people of any age. The good news is that malaria can be prevented and, if caught early, can be fully cured with proper medical treatment. Left untreated, however, malaria can become severe and even life-threatening, especially in young children, pregnant women, and people with weak immunity.

Early recognition of symptoms and prompt treatment at a health facility are the most important steps in preventing serious illness or death from malaria. Common Symptoms
Malaria symptoms usually appear about one to two weeks after the bite of an infected mosquito, though in some cases it can take longer. Common symptoms include:
Sudden high fever, often with shivering and chills
Heavy sweating as the fever breaks
Headache and body aches
Nausea and vomiting
Tiredness and weakness
Loss of appetite
A common pattern in malaria is a fever cycle: the person may first feel cold and shiver, then develop a high fever, and later sweat heavily as the fever comes down. This cycle may repeat every day or every few days depending on the type of malaria.

This cycle may repeat every day or every few days depending on the type of malaria. Because early symptoms are similar to common flu or viral fever, malaria can be easily missed unless a blood test is done. Anyone with fever in a malaria-prone area should get tested rather than assume it is an ordinary fever. Causes
Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite that spreads through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. These mosquitoes are most active at night and during dusk and dawn hours. They breed in stagnant water found in ponds, puddles, paddy fields, ditches, and other water collections, especially in forested, hilly, and rural areas.

When an infected mosquito bites a person, the parasite enters the bloodstream and multiplies in the liver before affecting the red blood cells, which is what causes fever and other symptoms. Malaria does not spread through coughing, touching, or sharing food or water with an infected person; it spreads only through the bite of an infected mosquito, and in rare cases through infected blood transfusions or contaminated needles. When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs – Act Immediately)
Any fever in a malaria-prone area should be checked by a health worker or doctor with a blood test as soon as possible, since early diagnosis and treatment give the best outcome.

Go to a doctor or hospital immediately, without delay, if the person has any of the following warning signs:
High fever that does not come down or keeps returning
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep fluids down
Extreme weakness or inability to stand or walk
Confusion, drowsiness, or difficulty staying awake
Convulsions or fits
Fast or difficult breathing
Yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice)
Very pale skin, palms, or eyes (signs of severe anaemia)
Dark or reduced urine output
Children under five, pregnant women, elderly people, and those with other health conditions are at higher risk of the illness turning severe quickly, so they should be taken for testing and treatment at the very first sign of fever rather than waiting to see if it improves on its own.

Home Care and Prevention
Home care (only for confirmed mild malaria under medical guidance):
Take complete rest and avoid strenuous work until fully recovered
Drink plenty of fluids – water, ORS, coconut water, or soup – to prevent dehydration
Eat light, nutritious food to support recovery
Take all medicines exactly as prescribed by the doctor, and complete the full course even if feeling better – stopping early can cause the illness to return or become harder to treat
Keep monitoring body temperature and overall condition, and return to the health centre if symptoms worsen
Prevention (avoiding mosquito bites and breeding):
Sleep under a mosquito net every night, especially insecticide-treated nets, even during the day for infants and young children
Use mosquito repellents and wear full-sleeved clothes, particularly in the evening and at night
Keep doors and windows screened or closed around dusk
Drain or treat stagnant water near homes, including puddles, ditches, and unused containers
Support local indoor residual spraying and larvicide programmes conducted by health workers
Get tested promptly for any fever, and inform the nearest health worker or ASHA if fever persists
Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha has historically been among the states in India most affected by malaria, with the burden concentrated in specific parts of the state rather than spread evenly.

Several tribal and forested districts, particularly in the southern, western, and northern belts of Odisha, have long recorded a higher number of malaria cases compared to the coastal districts. These areas tend to have hilly, forested terrain, scattered and remote habitations, and a warm, humid climate, all of which favour mosquito breeding and make regular healthcare access more difficult for some communities. Because of this pattern, the state government and national health programmes have run focused malaria control and elimination efforts in these high-burden tribal and forested districts, including distribution of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, indoor spraying, and community-based screening and treatment camps carried out with the help of local health workers and ASHAs.

Residents of these regions, and anyone travelling to or working in forested and rural parts of Odisha, should take mosquito bite prevention seriously and seek prompt testing for any fever rather than waiting, since early detection greatly improves treatment outcomes. Continued community participation in net use, water management, and reporting of fever cases remains central to reducing malaria's impact in these regions. Source Basis

Mamata Yojana
Odisha's Maternity Benefit Scheme, Explained Simply
A Public Awareness Reference Guide
Important update: Since April 2025, the Odisha Mamata scheme has been merged with the central Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) into a combined "Mamata-PMMVY" scheme, with revised cash amounts. Readers should confirm on the official Odisha Women and Child Development portal whether they will be enrolled as "Mamata" or "Mamata-PMMVY", as names, forms, and amounts may have changed further since this document was written. 1. Overview
Mamata Yojana is a maternity benefit scheme run by the Government of Odisha, first launched in 2011 by the Department of Women and Child Development.

It is a conditional cash transfer scheme, which means eligible women receive money directly into their bank account, provided they complete certain health-related steps during pregnancy and after childbirth. The scheme's main purpose is to reduce malnutrition among mothers and infants, and to lower maternal and infant deaths in the state. It does this by giving pregnant and lactating women partial compensation for the wages they may lose while resting during pregnancy and early motherhood, and by encouraging them to attend antenatal check-ups, deliver in a health facility, and get their child immunised on time. The scheme works through the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) network and is implemented through Anganwadi Centres across all districts of Odisha. 2.

2. Eligibility
Pregnant and lactating women aged 19 years or above are eligible for the scheme. Benefits are generally available for a woman's first two live births. Women who are themselves government or public sector employees, or whose husbands are government or public sector employees, and who are therefore eligible for maternity benefits through their employer, are usually excluded from this scheme. As part of the scheme's integration with the central PMMVY programme, additional eligibility routes may apply for women from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, women with disabilities, ration card holders, e-Shram card holders, and women covered under related welfare schemes, regardless of the two-child condition in some cases.

Because eligibility conditions have been updated as part of the recent merger with PMMVY, and can vary based on individual circumstances, pregnant women should confirm their specific eligibility with their local Anganwadi Worker or Child Development Project Officer (CDPO). 3. Benefits
Mamata Yojana provides cash assistance in return for completing specific health and nutrition-related steps during pregnancy and after childbirth, such as early registration of pregnancy, antenatal check-ups, institutional delivery, and timely immunisation of the child. Under the combined Mamata-PMMVY scheme, eligible mothers are reported to receive Rs. 10,000 for the birth of a boy, and an enhanced amount of Rs. 12,000 for the birth of a girl, paid in instalments linked to specific conditions being met.

12,000 for the birth of a girl, paid in instalments linked to specific conditions being met. Women belonging to Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) are reported to receive enhanced support of Rs. 12,000 for a girl child and Rs. 10,000 for a boy, for all live births, recognising the additional health vulnerabilities faced by these communities. Payments are made directly into the beneficiary's bank account through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), reducing delays and the need for cash handling. Alongside cash assistance, beneficiaries are supported with nutrition counselling, tracking through the Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card, and guidance from Anganwadi Workers and ASHA workers throughout pregnancy and early childcare.

Because cash amounts, instalment structures, and eligibility-linked conditions can be revised by the state government from time to time, beneficiaries should confirm the current benefit structure with their Anganwadi Centre or the official scheme portal before relying on any specific figure. 4. How to Apply
As soon as pregnancy is confirmed, visit the nearest Anganwadi Centre and inform the Anganwadi Worker, ideally within the first few months of pregnancy. The Anganwadi Worker or supervising Child Development Project Officer (CDPO) will typically carry out registration for the scheme, based on details such as age, number of live births, identity proof, and bank account information.

Keep the Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card and other identity documents, such as Aadhaar, ration card, or e-Shram card if applicable, ready, as these are commonly used to verify eligibility. Complete the required antenatal check-ups, opt for institutional delivery where possible, and ensure the child's immunisation is completed on schedule, since these steps are usually linked to the release of instalments. Once each required condition is verified, the applicable instalment is expected to be transferred directly to the registered bank account.

For questions, missed registration, or delayed payments, beneficiaries can approach their local Anganwadi Centre, the CDPO office, or check the official Mamata-PMMVY portal maintained by the Department of Women and Child Development, Government of Odisha. 5. Source Basis

Maternal Health Awareness
A Public Health Awareness Reference on Pregnancy Care, Antenatal Checkups, and Safe Delivery
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Maternal health refers to the health and well-being of women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the period after delivery. Good maternal health care helps protect the life of both the mother and the baby, and reduces the risk of serious complications that can occur before, during, or after childbirth. Regular antenatal check-ups, safe and timely delivery at a proper health facility, and good care after birth are the three pillars of safe motherhood.

Many maternal and newborn deaths can be prevented when pregnant women receive timely, quality care from trained health workers throughout this journey. This document provides general awareness on basic pregnancy care, the importance of regular antenatal care (ANC) checkups, and why delivering at a health facility (institutional delivery) is safer than delivering at home.

Key Practices
Antenatal Care (ANC) Checkups
Register the pregnancy early with the local health centre or ASHA worker as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Attend all recommended antenatal check-ups through the pregnancy, as advised by health workers, so that the mother's health and the baby's growth can be monitored regularly
Get routine blood pressure, weight, blood, and urine checks at each visit to catch early signs of complications
Take iron, folic acid, and calcium supplements as advised by a health worker or doctor, and complete the recommended tetanus toxoid vaccination doses
Discuss any unusual symptoms, discomfort, or concerns with the health worker or doctor during each visit
Make use of free antenatal check-up days offered at government health facilities every month
Basic Pregnancy Care
Eat a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, fruits, pulses, and iron-rich foods to support the growing baby
Get adequate rest and avoid heavy physical strain, especially in the later months of pregnancy
Drink enough clean, safe water through the day
Avoid tobacco, alcohol, and any medicines not advised by a doctor
Maintain good hygiene and attend to any infections or illness promptly with medical advice
Prepare a simple birth plan in advance, including which health facility to go to, how to reach it, and who will accompany the mother
Institutional Delivery
Plan to deliver at a hospital, Community Health Centre (CHC), Primary Health Centre (PHC), or other proper health facility with trained staff, rather than at home
Identify the nearest facility offering delivery services well before the expected date, and know how transport will be arranged
Keep all antenatal records, the mother and child health (MCH) card, and identification documents ready in advance
Seek care immediately if labour pains, bleeding, or waters breaking begin, and do not delay travel to the health facility
After Delivery (Postnatal Care)
Attend postnatal check-ups for both mother and newborn as advised by health workers
Begin breastfeeding as early as possible after birth, and continue exclusive breastfeeding as advised
Ensure the newborn receives recommended vaccinations on schedule
Watch for warning signs in the mother, such as heavy bleeding, high fever, or severe weakness, and seek medical help immediately if these occur
Why It Matters
Pregnancy and childbirth can involve serious health risks if complications are not identified and managed in time.

Regular antenatal check-ups allow health workers to detect problems such as high blood pressure, anaemia, or abnormal growth of the baby early, when they are easier to manage. Delivering at a proper health facility, attended by trained doctors, nurses, or midwives, greatly reduces the risk of complications during childbirth. Health facilities are equipped to handle emergencies such as heavy bleeding, obstructed labour, or newborn distress, which can be life-threatening if they occur at home without medical support. Good maternal health care benefits not only the mother but also the long-term health and development of the child. Timely care during pregnancy, safe delivery, and proper care afterward together form the foundation of a healthy start for both mother and baby.

Monsoon Season Health Precautions
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
The monsoon season brings much-needed rain, but it also creates conditions where certain illnesses spread more easily. Heavy rain, waterlogging, and humidity allow disease-causing germs and mosquitoes to multiply quickly, while flooding can contaminate drinking water sources and food. The most common health problems during the monsoon include water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid, and cholera, and mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria, dengue, and chikungunya. Skin infections and food poisoning also become more common in this season.

Skin infections and food poisoning also become more common in this season. Most of these illnesses can be prevented through simple precautions related to safe water, mosquito control, food safety, and general hygiene. Being aware of these risks and acting early can protect individuals, families, and entire communities during the rainy months.

Key Practices
Water-Borne Disease Prevention
Drink only clean, safe water; boil water if its safety is uncertain, especially after heavy rain or flooding
Store drinking water in a clean, covered container, and avoid drawing water with hands or unclean utensils
Avoid drinking water from open wells, ponds, or sources that may be contaminated by floodwater or overflow from drains
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
If diarrhoea occurs, give plenty of fluids and oral rehydration solution to prevent dehydration, and seek medical care promptly, especially for children and the elderly
Mosquito Control
Do not allow water to collect or stagnate in and around the house, including in pots, tyres, coolers, and containers
Empty, clean, and dry water-storage containers regularly to stop mosquitoes from breeding
Use mosquito nets while sleeping, and use screens on doors and windows where possible
Wear full-sleeved clothing, especially during early morning and evening hours when mosquitoes are most active
Use mosquito repellents and coils as needed, particularly for children and pregnant women
Support local mosquito-control efforts such as fogging and larvicide spraying carried out by health workers
Food Safety
Eat freshly cooked, hot food, and avoid food that has been left uncovered or exposed to flies
Wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly with clean water before eating or cooking
Avoid street food and cut fruit sold in the open during the monsoon, as these are more likely to carry germs
Store cooked food properly and avoid eating leftovers that have been kept for long periods without refrigeration
Keep kitchen areas clean and free from flies, pests, and stagnant water
General Precautions
Avoid wading through floodwater where possible; wash feet and legs thoroughly with soap if contact cannot be avoided
Rest and stay hydrated if feeling unwell, and avoid self-treating fever that lasts more than two to three days
Seek medical care promptly for high fever, severe body ache, persistent vomiting, or signs of dehydration
Keep the surroundings of the home clean, and ensure proper drainage to avoid waterlogging
Why It Matters
During the monsoon, contaminated water and food become a major route for diseases like diarrhoea, typhoid, and cholera to spread within families and communities, particularly affecting young children and the elderly, who are more vulnerable to dehydration and complications.

At the same time, stagnant water created by the rains becomes an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes that spread malaria, dengue, and chikungunya. These illnesses can cause high fever, severe body pain, and in some cases serious complications, so early recognition and prompt medical attention are important. Because many monsoon illnesses share similar symptoms, such as fever and body ache, it is important not to self-diagnose. A visit to the nearest health centre for proper testing is the safest way to identify the illness and begin the right care in time. Community-level prevention, such as controlling mosquito breeding sites and maintaining clean drainage, is often more effective than individual precautions alone, so cooperating with local health and sanitation efforts benefits everyone.

Odisha-Specific Context
Odisha's monsoon season, driven mainly by the South-West monsoon, typically brings heavy rainfall between June and September, along with the risk of cyclones, particularly in coastal areas. The state is among the more flood-prone regions of the country, and low-lying and riverine districts are especially vulnerable to waterlogging and flash floods during this period.

Coastal and riverine districts, including those along the Mahanadi and other major rivers, are more prone to flooding, waterlogging, and disruption of safe drinking water supply during heavy rains
Following floods or cyclones, health authorities in Odisha have at times issued alerts for water-borne illnesses such as diarrhoea in affected districts, along with deployment of medical teams and preventive measures
The state government works with district health teams, ASHA workers, and disaster management authorities to carry out disease surveillance, chlorination of drinking water sources, and mosquito control activities during and after the monsoon
Residents in flood-prone and low-lying areas are encouraged to store extra clean drinking water when heavy rain is forecast, keep essential medicines on hand, and know the location of the nearest health facility or emergency shelter
Following updates from local authorities, the Indian Meteorological Department, and the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority during periods of heavy rainfall or cyclone warnings can help families prepare in advance
Being prepared ahead of the monsoon and following basic precautions can greatly reduce health risks for families across Odisha's rural, coastal, and flood-prone areas.

Basic Nutrition Guidance for Families
A Public Health Awareness Reference

Overview
Good nutrition means eating a variety of foods in the right amounts to keep the body healthy, active, and able to fight illness. What a family eats every day has a direct effect on the growth of children, the strength of working adults, and the health of pregnant women and elderly family members. A healthy diet does not need to be expensive or complicated. It simply means eating a balanced mix of foods, avoiding excess sugar, salt, and oil, and making the most of foods that are already available locally.

Poor nutrition, whether from eating too little or eating an unbalanced diet, can lead to problems such as poor growth in children, weakness, low immunity, and a higher risk of long-term diseases like diabetes and heart disease in adults. This document offers simple, general guidance on healthy eating for the whole family, along with information on why nutrition matters and how local food traditions can support good health.

Key Practices
Eat a Variety of Foods
Include foods from different groups at each meal: cereals (rice, wheat, millets), pulses (dal, beans), vegetables, fruits, and where possible, milk, eggs, or meat
Eat a mix of colours of fruits and vegetables, as different colours provide different vitamins and minerals
Use a combination of cereals and pulses (such as rice and dal) together, as this improves the quality of protein in the meal
Balance the Plate
Fill about half the plate with vegetables and fruits
Include a portion of whole grains such as rice, wheat, or millets
Add a portion of pulses, beans, eggs, fish, or meat for protein, based on what is available and affordable
Use oil and ghee in moderation rather than in excess
Limit Salt, Sugar, and Oil
Reduce added salt in cooking and avoid excess salty snacks, pickles, and papad
Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and packaged snacks
Choose boiled, steamed, or lightly cooked foods over deep-fried foods when possible
Special Attention for Vulnerable Groups
Young children need frequent, small meals with a variety of foods to support healthy growth
Breastfeeding is recommended for infants in the first months of life, along with timely introduction of a variety of foods as the child grows
Pregnant and breastfeeding women need extra nutritious food, including iron- and protein-rich foods, to support their own health and their child's growth
Elderly family members should be encouraged to eat soft, easily digestible, nutrient-rich foods and to stay well hydrated
General Habits
Eat meals at regular times and avoid skipping meals
Drink enough clean water through the day
Wash fruits and vegetables well before eating or cooking
Where possible, grow a small kitchen garden with vegetables and leafy greens for fresh, affordable nutrition
Why It Matters
Good nutrition supports healthy growth in children, helps prevent illness, and gives the body strength for daily work and study.

Malnutrition, whether from too little food or an unbalanced diet, can affect a child's physical growth and ability to learn, and can weaken the immune system, making infections more likely. At the same time, unhealthy eating habits, such as excess salt, sugar, and oily food, contribute to long-term health problems including high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease. Following a balanced diet from childhood through old age helps reduce the risk of these conditions later in life. Proper nutrition is especially important during pregnancy, early childhood, and adolescence, as these are periods of rapid growth and development. Good nutrition in these stages has a lasting impact on health across a person's lifetime.

Good nutrition in these stages has a lasting impact on health across a person's lifetime. Odisha-Specific Context

Traditional millets such as ragi (mandia), suan, and kangu are climate-resilient, nutrient-rich grains that have long been part of the diet in Odisha's tribal and rainfed regions

Families are encouraged to combine traditional foods like rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, and millets to create balanced, affordable, and locally accessible meals
Making the most of these local foods is an easy and culturally familiar way for Odisha families to support good nutrition at home.

Pneumonia in Children — A Public Health Reference Guide
Health awareness chatbot knowledge base entry
Overview
Pneumonia is an infection that affects the lungs of a child. It happens when germs — usually a virus or bacteria — enter the small air sacs of the lungs and cause them to fill with fluid or pus. This makes it hard for the child to breathe properly and get enough oxygen. Pneumonia is one of the leading causes of illness and death among young children in India and around the world, especially children under five years of age. Most children recover fully if the illness is noticed early and proper care is sought quickly. Many deaths from pneumonia can be prevented through awareness, timely treatment, and good nutrition.

Many deaths from pneumonia can be prevented through awareness, timely treatment, and good nutrition. Common Symptoms
Symptoms can appear suddenly or develop over a day or two. Parents and caregivers should watch for:
Cough, which may be dry or produce mucus
Fast or difficult breathing
Fever, sometimes with chills or sweating
Fatigue, weakness, or unusual sleepiness
Loss of appetite or refusal to feed (in infants)
Chest pain, especially when breathing or coughing
In babies and toddlers: pale or limp appearance, and more crying than usual
A child with pneumonia often looks more unwell than a child with an ordinary cold, and the breathing difficulty tends to stand out as the most important warning sign.

Causes
Pneumonia in children is usually caused by:
Viruses — such as those causing the common cold, influenza, or RSV; these are the most frequent cause in young children
Bacteria — including pneumococcus, which can cause more serious illness
Sometimes a viral infection weakens the airway or immune system, allowing bacteria to grow and cause a second infection
Certain factors make children more vulnerable to pneumonia, including young age (especially newborns), low birth weight, poor nutrition, incomplete vaccination, indoor smoke from cooking fires, air pollution, overcrowded living conditions, and lack of clean water and sanitation. When to See a Doctor — Red-Flag Warning Signs
Early recognition saves lives.

When to See a Doctor — Red-Flag Warning Signs
Early recognition saves lives. Take the child to a health worker, clinic, or hospital immediately if any of the following are seen:
Fast or unusually difficult breathing
The lower chest sinks in or pulls inward when the child breathes in (chest indrawing)
Grunting sounds while breathing, or flaring of the nostrils
Bluish or grey colour on the lips, face, or fingertips
The child is unable to drink, breastfeed, or keep fluids down
Unusual sleepiness, difficulty waking the child, or reduced alertness
Convulsions or fits
High fever that does not improve, or fever in an infant under two months
Symptoms that are getting worse instead of better after a day or two
These are danger signs that need urgent medical attention without delay.
Do not wait to see if the child improves on their own — a delay of even a few hours can be serious for a young child with severe pneumonia.

Home Care and Prevention
While waiting to see a health worker, or for milder illness being monitored by a doctor, simple supportive care helps a child feel better:
Encourage plenty of rest
Offer fluids often — water, breast milk, or usual foods — to prevent dehydration
Keep the child warm but not overheated, and in a comfortable, well-ventilated room
Continue breastfeeding infants; keep offering small, frequent meals to older children
Avoid exposure to smoke, including cooking smoke and tobacco smoke
Always consult a qualified doctor or health worker before giving any medicine, and follow their advice fully
Prevention is the most powerful tool against childhood pneumonia:
Complete all recommended childhood vaccinations on schedule, including those that protect against pneumonia-causing germs
Practice exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, and continue breastfeeding alongside other foods afterward
Ensure good nutrition to keep the child's immune system strong
Wash hands regularly with soap, especially before feeding and after using the toilet
Reduce indoor air pollution by using cleaner cooking fuel and ensuring good ventilation
Keep children away from people who have coughs, colds, or flu-like symptoms where possible
Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha's Health and Family Welfare Department, through the National Health Mission (NHM) Odisha, runs the SAANS initiative (Social Awareness and Actions to Neutralize Pneumonia Successfully).

This programme trains frontline health workers to identify and treat childhood pneumonia early and ensures that treatment is available closer to communities. The state has also strengthened child health services through Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) units at newborn care centres, Nutritional Rehabilitation Centres (NRCs) for severely malnourished children, and Paediatric ICUs at major medical college hospitals for children with severe illness. Odisha has achieved strong immunization coverage under Mission Indradhanush, which includes vaccines that help protect against pneumonia.

Families in Odisha, particularly in rural and tribal areas, are encouraged to seek care promptly at the nearest Anganwadi centre, sub-centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital if a child shows any warning signs described above. Public Healthcare Facilities in Puri District, Odisha
A Structured Reference Guide to District, Community, and Primary Health Facilities
Overview
Puri district, best known as the seat of the Jagannath Temple and a major pilgrimage and coastal destination, is served by a tiered public healthcare network under the Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare, coordinated locally by the Chief District Medical Officer (CDMO), Puri. The system follows the standard national structure: village-level Sub-Centres feed into Primary Health Centres (PHCs), which refer upward to Community Health Centres (CHCs) at the block level, which in turn refer to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHH) as the district's main secondary-level referral point.

Puri city is also home to Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital (SJMCH), a government medical college established in 2021, which adds a tertiary-care teaching hospital tier above the DHH. This overall structure follows the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) through the National Health Mission (NHM) and most recently revised in 2022. Facility Types
District Headquarters Hospital (DHH), Puri
DHH Puri, originally known as the Puri Pilgrimage Hospital, was rebuilt in 1909-10 and remains one of the district's oldest and most established public health institutions. It has the distinction of being among the first district hospitals in Odisha, and the second in India, to receive ISO 9001:2008 quality management certification.

As the district's secondary-level referral hospital, it is designed to receive cases referred from CHCs, PHCs, and Sub-Centres across all of Puri district's blocks, and given the district's high pilgrim and tourist footfall, it also plays an important role in handling visitor health emergencies alongside routine district referral care. Community Health Centres (CHCs)
CHCs are block-level referral units, generally serving a population of roughly 80,000 to 120,000 people. Puri district's blocks — including Kanas, Gop, Chandanpur/Nimapara area, Brahmagiri, Satyabadi, Astaranga, Delanga, Pipili, and others — each have a CHC that acts as the referral hub for the PHCs and Sub-Centres within that block.

For example, CHC Kanas, established in 1962, is a 24x7 facility (non-FRU) overseeing five PHCs and twenty-three Sub-Centres in its block, and is ISO 9001:2015 certified, illustrating the level of service standardization found at some CHCs in the district. A CHC is expected to have around 30 inpatient beds, an operation theatre, basic diagnostic and blood storage facilities, and specialist coverage in medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynaecology, and paediatrics, though actual staffing varies by centre; centres equipped for round-the-clock emergency obstetric and newborn care may be designated First Referral Units (FRUs).

Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
PHCs are typically the first point of contact with a qualified doctor for rural and semi-urban residents, each covering a population of around 20,000 to 30,000. Puri district has numerous PHCs and newer PHC(New) facilities distributed across its blocks — for instance, Astaranga block alone has several PHC(New) units in addition to its main PHC. Each PHC supervises a cluster of Sub-Centres, provides outpatient consultation, a small number of inpatient beds, basic laboratory testing, and normal delivery services at PHCs designated for 24x7 care, and oversees ASHA and ANM workers at the village level.

Sub-Centres and Health & Wellness Centres
Below the PHC level, Health Sub-Centres — increasingly upgraded as Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) — are the most peripheral public facilities, generally staffed by an ANM and a Community Health Officer. They handle preventive and promotive care such as immunization and antenatal check-ups, referring more complex cases upward to the PHC.

What Each Facility Handles
District Headquarters Hospital
Complex and emergency cases referred from CHCs and PHCs across the district
Broader specialist consultation and surgical services than block-level facilities
Diagnostics, blood storage/blood bank services, and larger inpatient bed capacity
Emergency care for pilgrims and tourists visiting Puri, alongside routine district referral cases
Possible empanelment under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat–PM-JAY for cashless treatment (current empanelment status should be verified locally)
Acts as the secondary-level referral hospital for the district, with onward referral to Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital or another tertiary centre for cases needing higher-level specialty care
Community Health Centres
Referral care for PHCs and Sub-Centres within the block, plus specialist consultation for patients approaching directly
Inpatient care (around 30 beds at fully staffed centres), minor and some major surgical procedures, and operation theatre services
Emergency obstetric care and institutional deliveries, particularly at 24x7-designated centres
Basic diagnostics including laboratory services and, at many centres, X-ray facilities
Primary Health Centres
Outpatient consultation for common illnesses, minor injuries, and chronic disease follow-up
Antenatal, natal, and postnatal care, including normal deliveries at 24x7 PHCs
Immunization, family planning services, and national health programme delivery (TB, malaria, non-communicable disease screening, and similar)
Basic laboratory tests (blood, urine, blood sugar, malaria rapid tests, and similar)
