How to Reach Them (General Guidance)
Since exact addresses and phone numbers are not being invented here, the following general approaches can help locate and reach the correct facility:
Ask the local ASHA worker, ANM, or Anganwadi worker — they know the nearest Sub-Centre and PHC serving a household and can help with referral upward if needed.

Every block headquarters in Puri district has a CHC (for example, Kanas, Gop, Chandanpur, Brahmagiri); the block administrative office can confirm its exact current location and status. The Puri district administration's official website and the CDMO Puri office maintain listings of health facilities; these should be treated as the authoritative source for confirmed addresses and phone numbers. The National Health Mission (NHM) Odisha and Odisha Directorate of Health Services websites publish facility directories and health scheme information at the state level. The 108 (emergency response) and 102 (patient transport / maternal-child) ambulance services can be used to reach an appropriate facility in an emergency, and can also help route a patient to the correct level of care.

For the District Headquarters Hospital specifically, and to distinguish it from Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital located separately in Puri city, confirm the current address and scope of services with the district health administration before travelling. Given Puri's high pilgrim and tourist traffic, visitors unfamiliar with the area should ask local authorities, hotel staff, or temple administration for the nearest functioning public health facility in an emergency.

When to Go to District Hospital vs PHC
Go to a PHC (or Sub-Centre) first for:
Routine illnesses — fever, cold, minor infections, common ailments
Antenatal check-ups, immunizations, and family planning services
Normal, uncomplicated deliveries at a 24x7-designated PHC
Basic diagnostic tests and follow-up for chronic conditions already under management
Minor injuries and first-aid level care
Go to (or be referred to) a CHC for:
Cases needing minor surgery, specialist consultation, or inpatient observation beyond what a PHC can provide
Complicated deliveries or emergency obstetric care, especially at a 24x7 or FRU-designated CHC
Situations where the PHC has stabilized a patient but recommended referral
Go directly to the District Headquarters Hospital for:
Serious emergencies — major trauma, accidents, severe medical emergencies where higher-level care is clearly needed
Conditions requiring specialist care, surgery, or diagnostics not available at PHC or CHC level
Cases already referred by a PHC or CHC as needing secondary-level hospital care
Health emergencies during pilgrimage seasons or large public gatherings, when DHH Puri is typically better equipped to handle higher patient volumes than a PHC
Situations covered under empanelled schemes (e.g., PM-JAY) requiring hospital-level admission — confirm current scheme coverage locally
As a general rule, the public health system is designed as a step-up referral chain: Sub-Centre → PHC → CHC → District Headquarters Hospital → Medical College Hospital, with each level equipped for progressively more complex care.

In Puri's case, DHH's long-established role and ISO certification make it a strong first stop for most secondary-level care, with Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital available for cases needing tertiary or specialized attention. Bypassing lower tiers is appropriate mainly in genuine emergencies, where reaching the nearest capable facility quickly — often via 108 ambulance services — matters more than following the tier order.

Skin Infections: Fungal and Bacterial
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Overview
Skin infections are among the most common health problems seen in India, especially in warm and humid regions. They happen when germs — either fungi or bacteria — grow on or inside the skin and cause irritation, discoloration, or sores. Most skin infections are not dangerous and can be managed with simple care and, when needed, a visit to a health worker or doctor. However, some infections can spread to other people or worsen if ignored, so early attention and good hygiene are important for the whole family and community.

Common Symptoms
Fungal skin infections (such as ringworm, athlete's foot, and jock itch) usually cause:
Itchy, red, ring-shaped or circular patches with a raised, scaly border
Peeling, cracking, or white/soggy skin, often between the toes or in skin folds
Patchy hair loss or scaling on the scalp in children
Discoloured, thickened, or crumbly nails
Bacterial skin infections (such as boils, impetigo, and cellulitis) usually cause:
Red, warm, swollen, and painful skin
Pus-filled boils or blisters that may ooze or crust over (often honey-coloured crusting)
Spreading redness or streaking around a wound or cut
Fever or feeling generally unwell in more serious cases
Causes
Fungal infections are caused by microscopic fungi that thrive in warm, moist, and sweaty conditions, such as skin folds, the groin, and between the toes.

They spread through direct skin contact, shared clothing, towels, combs, footwear, or contact with infected animals. Bacterial infections are usually caused by common skin bacteria entering through a cut, insect bite, scrape, or existing skin irritation. Poor hand hygiene, overcrowded living conditions, and scratching an itchy area can all increase the chance of bacteria entering the skin. Both types of infection are more likely when the skin stays wet or sweaty for long periods, when clothing is tight or unwashed, when personal items are shared, or when a person's overall health or immunity is weakened, for example due to diabetes or malnutrition.

When to See a Doctor (Red Flags)
Most mild skin infections can be cared for at home, but a person should see a doctor or visit the nearest health centre promptly if any of the following occur:
Fever, chills, or feeling very unwell along with a skin problem
Rapidly spreading redness, swelling, or warmth, especially with red streaks
Large, painful, or multiple boils, or pus that keeps increasing
Infection near the eyes, face, or genitals
No improvement after 1–2 weeks of basic home care
Infection in a person with diabetes, a weak immune system, or in a young infant
Signs of the infection spreading to other family members repeatedly
Deep or worsening wound, ulcer, or skin breakdown
Home Care and Prevention
Keep the affected area clean and completely dry, especially skin folds, groin, and between the toes
Wear loose, breathable cotton clothing and change out of sweaty clothes promptly
Bathe regularly and dry the body fully, particularly after sweating, farm work, or getting wet in the rain
Do not share towels, clothes, combs, footwear, or bedding with others
Avoid scratching affected skin, as this can spread infection and cause bacterial infection on top of a fungal one
Wash hands regularly, and clean any cuts or wounds promptly and keep them covered
Wash clothing, towels, and bedding in hot water and dry them well, ideally in sunlight
Drink enough water and eat a balanced diet to support the body's natural healing
Get adequate rest, especially if there is fever or general illness alongside the skin problem
Do not use any cream, ointment, or medicine without guidance from a qualified health worker or doctor
Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha's climate — long periods of high heat combined with high humidity, especially from summer through the monsoon season — creates ideal conditions for fungal skin infections to develop and spread.

Heavy sweating in this weather keeps skin folds, feet, and the groin area damp for long periods, which allows fungi to multiply more easily. Health data from parts of the state has shown that fungal skin infection cases rise noticeably between the middle of summer and the middle of the monsoon season, when temperatures and humidity are both at their highest. People who work outdoors, in agriculture, fishing, or manual labour, and those living in crowded households, may face a higher risk due to prolonged sweating, shared water sources, and limited access to frequent bathing or clean, dry clothing.

During Odisha's hot and humid months, extra attention to keeping the skin clean and dry, wearing breathable clothing, avoiding tight synthetic fabrics, and seeking care early at the nearest sub-centre, primary health centre, or community health worker can help reduce the spread and severity of these infections within families and communities. Tuberculosis (TB)
A Public Health Awareness Reference
For community health awareness use • Simple language for rural readers
Overview
Tuberculosis, commonly called TB, is a disease caused by germs (bacteria) called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most often affects the lungs, but it can also affect other parts of the body such as the bones, kidneys, brain, or lymph nodes. TB spreads through the air when a person with active TB disease in the lungs coughs, sneezes, or speaks. It does not spread by sharing food, water, utensils, or by touching someone. Not everyone who breathes in TB germs becomes sick — many people carry the germs in an inactive form without any symptoms and cannot spread it to others. Only when the germs become active does a person develop TB disease and become infectious.

Only when the germs become active does a person develop TB disease and become infectious. TB is both preventable and curable. With early diagnosis and a complete course of treatment, almost all people with TB can be fully cured. Delaying treatment increases the risk of the disease spreading to family members and worsening the patient's health.

Common Symptoms
TB should be suspected when a person has any of the following symptoms, especially if they last more than two to three weeks:
Cough lasting more than two weeks, which may bring up mucus or blood
Fever, especially low-grade fever that continues for many days
Night sweats
Unexplained weight loss
Loss of appetite
Ongoing tiredness or weakness
Chest pain, particularly with breathing or coughing
Swelling in the neck or elsewhere, if TB affects the lymph nodes
Symptoms can develop slowly and may be mild at first, which is why people sometimes delay seeking care. Any person with a persistent cough of two weeks or more should get tested for TB. Causes
TB is caused by infection with TB bacteria and spreads person to person through the air.

Causes
TB is caused by infection with TB bacteria and spreads person to person through the air. Key points about how it spreads and who is at higher risk:
TB spreads when an infectious person coughs, sneezes, or speaks and releases germs into the air, which another person then breathes in
Close, prolonged contact with someone who has active lung TB — such as living in the same household — increases the risk of infection
Crowded or poorly ventilated living and working spaces make it easier for TB to spread
People with weaker immune systems are at higher risk of developing TB disease after infection, including those living with HIV, people with diabetes, people who are malnourished, and people who use tobacco or alcohol heavily
Children, elderly people, and those with chronic illness are more vulnerable to severe disease
It is important to remember that TB is a curable illness caused by germs — it is not caused by any curse, sin, or personal failing, and people with TB should not be shunned or discriminated against.

When to See a Doctor — Red Flag Signs
Visit the nearest government health centre, ASHA worker, or hospital for TB testing without delay if you or a family member has any of the following:
Cough lasting two weeks or more
Blood in sputum (coughed-up mucus)
Fever that continues for more than two weeks, especially with night sweats
Unexplained weight loss or ongoing loss of appetite
Chest pain along with cough or breathing difficulty
Persistent tiredness and weakness that does not improve with rest
A known close contact (family member or household member) recently diagnosed with TB, even without symptoms yet
Children with poor weight gain, prolonged fever, or swelling in the neck glands
Difficulty breathing or coughing up blood in large amounts — seek emergency care immediately
TB testing (such as sputum tests and chest X-ray) and treatment are available free of cost at government TB centres and health facilities.

Do not wait for symptoms to worsen — early testing leads to faster cure and stops the disease from spreading to others. Home Care and Prevention
Care during TB treatment
Take the full course of treatment exactly as advised by the health worker or doctor, even after feeling better — stopping early can make the disease harder to cure and can lead to drug-resistant TB. Attend all follow-up visits and tests as scheduled. Eat a nutritious diet with enough protein, fruits, and vegetables, as advised by the health worker, to support recovery. Get adequate rest, especially in the early weeks of treatment. Cover the mouth and nose with a cloth or mask while coughing or sneezing, and dispose of used tissues safely.

Keep the room well ventilated by opening windows and doors to let in fresh air and sunlight. Avoid alcohol and tobacco use during treatment, as these can affect recovery. Do not stop or change medicines without consulting the treating doctor or health worker. Family members and close contacts should also get screened for TB, especially if they develop any symptoms. Prevention
Ensure infants receive the BCG vaccine, which is given under the national immunisation programme and helps protect young children from severe forms of TB. Keep living and working spaces well ventilated with good airflow and sunlight. Avoid crowded, poorly ventilated spaces where possible, especially if someone nearby has an active cough.

Maintain good nutrition, as undernourishment increases the risk of developing TB disease. If living with someone who has TB, follow the health worker's advice on precautions and get screened as a household contact. Complete any preventive treatment recommended by a health worker for people at higher risk, such as household contacts or people living with HIV. Seek prompt testing and treatment for anyone with prolonged cough or other symptoms — early treatment protects the whole family and community. Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha implements the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), including special campaigns to find and treat TB early, with particular attention to tribal, mining, and hard-to-reach districts of the state.

Free TB testing, chest X-ray, and treatment are available at government health facilities across Odisha, including Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and District TB Centres. The State TB Cell, under the Directorate of Public Health, Department of Health & Family Welfare, Government of Odisha, coordinates TB screening campaigns across all districts, including door-to-door and camp-based screening drives. Odisha has several tribal-dominated and mining districts identified as high priority under the national programme; residents of these areas are encouraged to get screened promptly if symptoms appear, as access to care can be more limited in remote pockets.

Community volunteers called Ni-kshay Mitras provide nutritional and other support to TB patients and their families in Odisha as part of the Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan. Patients registered for treatment may be eligible for a monthly nutritional support benefit under the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana, transferred directly to their bank account. Contact your nearest ASHA worker, ANM, Sub-Centre, or PHC for free TB screening, or call the Odisha health helpline in case of doubt or difficulty accessing care. India's TB Elimination Program
India runs the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, working towards the goal of eliminating TB ahead of global timelines.

The Ni-kshay portal is the national system used by health workers to register TB patients, track testing and treatment, and connect patients with support services. Under this programme and related initiatives such as the Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, testing and treatment for TB are provided completely free of cost at government health facilities, and additional nutritional and community support is available to registered patients through schemes like the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana and community volunteers known as Ni-kshay Mitras. Anyone with TB symptoms is encouraged to visit their nearest government health facility for free testing and care.

Typhoid Fever — A Public Health Reference Guide
Health awareness chatbot knowledge base entry
Overview
Typhoid fever is a serious illness caused by bacteria called Salmonella Typhi. It spreads mainly through food and water that have been contaminated with the germ, usually through unsafe handling of human waste. The bacteria enter the body through the mouth, travel through the gut, and then spread into the bloodstream, causing fever and illness throughout the body. Typhoid is common in areas with unsafe drinking water and poor sanitation, and it remains a public health concern in many parts of India, including Odisha. It can affect people of any age, but children and young adults are frequently affected. With timely medical care, most people recover fully.

With timely medical care, most people recover fully. Without proper treatment, typhoid can become severe and, in rare cases, life-threatening. Common Symptoms
Typhoid usually develops slowly, with symptoms appearing about one to three weeks after exposure to the bacteria. Common signs include:
Fever that starts low and gradually rises over several days, often becoming very high
Persistent headache
Weakness, fatigue, and body aches
Loss of appetite
Stomach pain or discomfort
Constipation or, in some people, loose stools
Nausea
In some cases, a rash of small flat, rose-coloured spots on the chest or abdomen
Symptoms often build up gradually rather than appearing suddenly, and the fever tends to stay high and does not go away with rest alone.

If untreated, symptoms can become more severe over the following weeks. Causes
Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, which lives only in humans. A person becomes infected mainly by:
Drinking water that has been contaminated with human waste
Eating food prepared or washed with contaminated water
Eating food handled by a person carrying the bacteria who did not wash their hands properly
Eating raw fruits or vegetables that were washed in unsafe water
Some people who recover from typhoid can continue to carry the bacteria in their body for a long time without feeling sick themselves, and can still spread it to others through poor hand hygiene.

This is why safe water, sanitation, and hygiene practices are so important in preventing typhoid, both for the sick person and for the wider community. When to See a Doctor — Red-Flag Warning Signs
Typhoid needs proper medical diagnosis and treatment. Do not try to manage it with home remedies alone.

Do not try to manage it with home remedies alone. See a doctor or health worker promptly if a person has:
Fever that continues for more than two to three days, especially if it keeps rising
High fever that does not improve with rest and fluids
Severe or worsening stomach pain
Ongoing vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down
Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools
Severe weakness, confusion, difficulty staying awake, or unusual drowsiness
Signs of dehydration, such as very little urine, dry mouth, or sunken eyes
Fast or difficult breathing
Fever in a young child, elderly person, pregnant woman, or anyone with an existing serious illness
These signs may point to a severe infection or a complication and need urgent medical attention.
Suspected typhoid should always be confirmed and treated by a qualified doctor, since correct treatment matters for full recovery and for preventing the person from spreading the infection to others.

Home Care and Prevention
If a doctor has diagnosed typhoid and is guiding treatment, simple supportive care at home can help the person feel better and recover:
Get plenty of rest
Drink plenty of clean, safe fluids to prevent dehydration, especially if there is fever or loose stools
Eat light, easily digestible food as appetite allows
Follow the doctor's advice fully and complete the full course of any treatment given, even if the person starts to feel better
Keep the sick person's utensils, clothing, and bedding separate, and wash them properly
Always wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before preparing or eating food, especially while someone in the household is unwell
Typhoid can largely be prevented by protecting water and food from contamination.

Households and communities can reduce risk by:
Drinking only safe water — boiled, filtered, or from a protected, tested source
Storing drinking water in a clean, covered container
Washing hands with soap before eating, before cooking, and after using the toilet
Washing fruits and vegetables with safe water before eating
Eating freshly cooked, hot food, and avoiding food from unhygienic surroundings
Using a proper toilet and avoiding open defecation
Asking a health worker about the typhoid vaccine, which is available in some immunization programmes for children and can offer added protection
Odisha-Specific Notes
In many rural parts of Odisha, drinking water still comes from tube wells, dug wells, or other sources that are not always tested or protected from contamination, and a large share of households do not treat their water before drinking it.

Studies from rural Odisha have also found that open defecation continues in some communities, which increases the risk of water and food contamination and the spread of typhoid and similar illnesses. There have also been local outbreaks reported in the state linked to contaminated water sources, underlining why safe water practices matter. Families in rural Odisha can protect themselves by always boiling or properly filtering drinking water, keeping water storage containers covered and clean, using a toilet instead of open defecation, and washing hands with soap at key times such as before meals and after using the toilet.

Government programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission (for safe piped water to rural households) and Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen (for sanitation and ending open defecation) support these efforts in Odisha. The National Health Mission, Odisha, along with ASHA and Anganwadi workers, also promotes hygiene education and can guide families on safe water and food practices and where to seek care. Anyone in Odisha with an unexplained continuing fever, especially during the monsoon or summer months when water contamination risk is higher, should visit the nearest sub-centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), or hospital rather than waiting for symptoms to worsen.

Viral Fever – Public Health Reference
Overview
Viral fever is a general term for fever caused by viruses... It usually improves within a few days with rest and fluids. Some serious illnesses such as dengue, malaria or bacterial infections can also start with fever, so persistent or severe symptoms need medical evaluation. Common Symptoms
Fever, chills, headache, body ache, tiredness, sore throat, cough, runny nose, loss of appetite, mild nausea. Symptoms vary depending on the virus. Causes
Spread through droplets, close contact, contaminated hands/surfaces, or by mosquitoes for some viral diseases. Seasonal changes can increase circulation of viruses.

Seasonal changes can increase circulation of viruses. When to See a Doctor
Seek medical care urgently for: difficulty breathing; confusion; persistent high fever; fever lasting more than 2–3 days or returning; severe dehydration; repeated vomiting; severe abdominal pain; seizures; rash with bleeding; pregnancy, infants, older adults, or people with serious illness developing fever. Home Care and Prevention
Rest well, drink plenty of safe fluids, eat light nutritious food, maintain hand hygiene, cover coughs/sneezes, avoid close contact while sick, use safe drinking water and mosquito control where appropriate, and follow medical advice. Odisha-specific notes
In Odisha, viral and mosquito-borne fevers commonly increase during the monsoon because of standing water and higher mosquito breeding.

During summer, dehydration and heat can occur along with seasonal viral illnesses. Any fever during these seasons should be monitored carefully because dengue, chikungunya and malaria may have similar early symptoms. Source basis

Understanding the Symptom: Vomiting
A general health awareness reference (not a diagnosis)
Symptom Overview
Vomiting means the stomach forcefully brings up its contents through the mouth. It is not a disease by itself — it is a sign that the body is reacting to something, such as an infection, food problem, motion, heat, or another illness. Vomiting can happen once or many times, and it may occur along with other symptoms like loose motion (diarrhoea), fever, stomach pain, weakness, or dizziness. In most cases vomiting settles on its own within a day or two, but sometimes it can lead to loss of body fluids and salts, which needs attention, especially in small children, elderly people, and pregnant women. Possible Common Causes
Vomiting can happen for many different reasons.

Possible Common Causes
Vomiting can happen for many different reasons. This list only describes possible everyday causes — it does not diagnose any illness. A doctor or health worker should be consulted to know the exact cause.

A doctor or health worker should be consulted to know the exact cause. Eating spoiled, stale, or contaminated food or drinking unsafe water
Stomach infections such as viral or bacterial gastroenteritis, which often also cause loose motion
Overeating, eating very oily or spicy food, or eating too fast
Motion sickness during travel by bus, car, or boat
Heat exhaustion or dehydration during hot weather
Pregnancy, especially in the early months (morning sickness)
Fever-related illness, including seasonal infections
Migraine or severe headache
Side effect of certain medicines
Emotional stress, anxiety, or strong smells
Self-Care Advice
If vomiting is mild and the person is otherwise alert and able to drink fluids, simple home care often helps:
Sip small amounts of water, ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution), or clean fluids frequently — do not drink a large amount at once, as this can trigger more vomiting
If ORS packets are available, mix as per the instructions on the packet and drink slowly through the day
If ORS is not available, a simple home fluid can be made using clean water with a little salt and sugar
Rest and avoid solid food for a few hours; once vomiting slows down, start with light food like rice water, banana, toast, or khichdi
Avoid oily, spicy, or heavy food until the stomach settles
For infants, continue breastfeeding; offer small sips of ORS in between feeds
Maintain hand hygiene and keep drinking water covered and clean to avoid spreading infection to others
Take rest in a cool, shaded place, especially during hot weather
When to Seek Medical Attention
Please visit the nearest health centre, sub-centre, or hospital without delay if any of the following are noticed:
⚠ Vomiting continues repeatedly for more than a day, or the person cannot keep any fluids down
⚠ Signs of dehydration: very little or no urine, dry mouth, sunken eyes, extreme thirst, or in infants, no tears when crying and a sunken soft spot on the head
⚠ Blood in the vomit, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
⚠ Severe stomach pain, high fever, or stiffness in the neck
⚠ Confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, or difficulty waking up
⚠ Vomiting after a head injury or fall
⚠ Vomiting in a small child, elderly person, or pregnant woman that does not improve quickly
⚠ Suspected poisoning or reaction after taking any medicine
These signs may point to a more serious condition and need to be checked by a qualified doctor or health worker as soon as possible.

Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, cases of vomiting and loose motion tend to rise during the summer heatwave months and again during the monsoon season. Extreme heat can cause dehydration, weakness, and vomiting, so drinking enough water, ORS, and lemon water, avoiding outdoor work during peak afternoon hours, and eating water-rich fruits are commonly advised during this period. During the monsoon, contaminated drinking water and poor sanitation can lead to outbreaks of diarrhoeal illness in some districts, and local health authorities may issue special alerts.

If vomiting occurs along with watery loose motion during such a period, especially if several people in the same household or village fall sick together, it is important to inform the local ASHA worker, sub-centre, or Primary Health Centre (PHC) promptly and to drink only boiled or safely treated water. Free ORS and basic treatment are usually available at government health facilities. Source Basis
